tension_pneumothorax.hook: Tension pneumothorax is a one-way valve physiology where air enters the pleural space during inspiration but cannot exit, causing progressive mediastinal shift that kinks the great veins and collapses the contralateral lung.
features: Hypotension with distended neck veins due to impaired venous return from mediastinal compression and kinking of the superior vena cava.
Tracheal deviation away from the affected side because the mediastinum is pushed contralaterally by the accumulating air under pressure.
Hyperresonance and absent breath sounds on the affected side with contralateral tracheal shift—a mechanical consequence of air trapped under tension, not lung pathology.
traps: Cardiac tamponade: Also causes hypotension and distended neck veins, but trachea is midline and breath sounds are equal; tamponade compresses the heart from all sides, not the mediastinum unilaterally.
Massive pulmonary embolism: Can present with hypotension and distended neck veins, but breath sounds are usually clear and trachea midline; the obstruction is vascular, not air-filled pleural space.
Simple pneumothorax: No hypotension or tracheal shift because there is no tension; intrapleural pressure is not high enough to impair venous return or shift the mediastinum.
tension_pneumothorax.clue: In a patient with acute chest pain and respiratory distress, the presence of hypotension, distended neck veins, and tracheal deviation away from the side of absent breath sounds is pathognomonic for tension pneumothorax and mandates immediate needle decompression.

aortic_dissection.hook: Aortic dissection causes chest pain through sudden tearing of the intima, creating a false lumen that can propagate and compromise branch vessels — unlike tension pneumothorax where pain is from pleural stretch and mediastinal shift.
features: Tearing or ripping quality of pain that may radiate to the back or interscapular region due to dissection along the aorta.
Pulse or blood pressure differential between arms from involvement of the subclavian or brachiocephalic arteries.
Neurologic deficits (e.g., stroke, Horner's) from carotid or sympathetic chain compromise by the expanding false lumen.
traps: Tension pneumothorax: both can cause sudden chest pain and respiratory distress, but tension pneumothorax features tracheal deviation, hyperresonance, and absent breath sounds on the affected side — not pulse deficits or neurologic signs.

Acute myocardial infarction: both present with chest pain and can show ECG changes, but dissection pain is typically tearing/ripping and may be associated with aortic regurgitation murmur or widened mediastinum on CXR.
Pulmonary embolism: both cause acute chest pain and dyspnea, but PE classically has pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, and signs of right heart strain on ECG/echo without pulse deficits.
aortic_dissection.clue: A pulse or blood pressure differential between the arms is the single most discriminating physical exam finding for aortic dissection.

asthma_exacerbation.hook: In tension pneumothorax, air trapped in the pleural space under positive pressure collapses the lung and shifts the mediastinum, obstructing venous return—this is a mechanical obstruction, not airway inflammation.
features: Sudden, pleuritic chest pain with ipsilateral hyperresonance and absent breath sounds due to air trapping and lung collapse.
Distended neck veins and hypotension from impaired right heart filling caused by mediastinal shift and increased intrathoracic pressure.
Tracheal deviation away from the affected side as the mediastinum is pushed contralaterally by the expanding air pocket.
traps: Asthma exacerbation: Diffuse wheezing from bronchoconstriction, not unilateral absent breath sounds; no tracheal deviation or hyperresonance.
Aortic dissection: Tearing chest pain radiating to back, often with pulse deficits or neurological signs; no hyperresonance or tracheal deviation.
Pulmonary embolism: Dyspnea and pleuritic pain but with normal breath sounds, no hyperresonance, and often hemoptysis or DVT history.
asthma_exacerbation.clue: Unilateral absent breath sounds with hyperresonance and tracheal deviation away from the affected side.

pneumothorax.hook: In tension pneumothorax, the one-way valve mechanism traps air in the pleural space, progressively shifting the mediastinum and compressing the contralateral lung and great vessels—this is why you see hypotension and distended neck veins, not just hypoxia.
features: Unilateral hyperresonance and absent breath sounds due to air trapping and lung collapse on the affected side
Tracheal deviation away from the affected side because the mediastinum is pushed contralaterally by rising intrapleural pressure
Hypotension and distended neck veins from impaired venous return as the mediastinal shift compresses the superior vena cava and right heart
traps: Aortic dissection: presents with tearing chest pain and pulse deficits, but breath sounds are symmetric and trachea midline; the mechanism is a tear in the aortic wall, not air in the pleural space.

Simple pneumothorax: has unilateral hyperresonance and decreased breath sounds but no hypotension or tracheal deviation because intrapleural pressure does not exceed atmospheric; the valve mechanism is absent.

Cardiac tamponade: also causes hypotension and distended neck veins, but breath sounds are symmetric and heart sounds are muffled; the mechanism is pericardial fluid compressing the heart, not mediastinal shift from pleural air.
pneumothorax.clue: In a patient with acute chest pain and respiratory distress, the presence of tracheal deviation away from the hyperresonant side on exam is pathognomonic for tension pneumothorax and demands immediate needle decompression.

pulmonary_embolism.hook: In PE, chest pain is pleuritic from subpleural infarction and dyspnea is out of proportion to exam—unlike tension pneumothorax where tracheal deviation and absent breath sounds create immediate mechanical obstruction.
features: Pleuritic chest pain that worsens with inspiration (subpleural lung infarction or inflammation).
Tachypnea with clear lungs initially—dyspnea exceeds auscultatory findings.
Signs of right heart strain (distended neck veins, RV heave) from acute pulmonary hypertension.
traps: Tension pneumothorax: tracheal deviation, hyperresonance, absent breath sounds—mechanical air trapping, not vascular occlusion.
Aortic dissection: tearing/ripping pain radiating to back, pulse deficits—due to aortic wall shear, not intraluminal clot.
Asthma exacerbation: diffuse wheezing, prolonged expiration—airway obstruction, not vascular obstruction.
pulmonary_embolism.clue: Sudden pleuritic chest pain with dyspnea out of proportion to lung exam and no tracheal deviation or hyperresonance.

angina.hook: Angina’s demand-supply mismatch is gradual and positional, whereas tension pneumothorax is a one-way valve trap that builds pressure until it crushes venous return — a physical, not ischemic, catastrophe.
features: Chest pain in angina is exertional, pressure-like, and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin; in tension pneumothorax, pain is pleuritic, sharp, and unrelieved by position.

Tension pneumothorax causes tracheal deviation away from the affected side, absent breath sounds, and distended neck veins — all due to mediastinal shift compressing the contralateral lung and great vessels.
Hypotension and tachycardia in tension pneumothorax stem from reduced preload (compressed vena cava), not from myocardial ischemia or pump failure as in angina.
traps: Aortic dissection: tearing pain radiating to the back, pulse deficits, and widened mediastinum — mechanism is intimal tear with false lumen, not air trapping under pressure.
Pulmonary embolism: sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, and hypoxia from clot obstruction, not tracheal deviation or ipsilateral hyperresonance.
Asthma exacerbation: diffuse wheezing and prolonged expiration from bronchoconstriction, not unilateral absent breath sounds or tracheal deviation.
angina.clue: Tracheal deviation away from the side of lung collapse with ipsilateral hyperresonance and absent breath sounds — this is pathognomonic for tension pneumothorax and absent in angina.

acute_pericarditis_idiopathic.hook: Acute pericarditis causes chest pain by inflammation of the pericardium, not by air trapping under tension compressing the heart and great vessels.
features: Chest pain that is pleuritic, positional (worse supine, better leaning forward), and may radiate to the trapezius ridge due to phrenic nerve irritation from inflamed pericardium.
Pericardial friction rub on auscultation, a scratchy sound caused by inflamed layers rubbing during cardiac motion.
Diffuse ST-segment elevation on ECG with PR depression, reflecting epicardial inflammation and injury current.
traps: Tension pneumothorax: presents with acute chest pain and respiratory distress, but pain is non-positional, unilateral, with absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, and tracheal deviation due to air under tension collapsing the lung and shifting mediastinum.
Aortic dissection: presents with severe tearing chest pain radiating to back, but pain is not pleuritic or positional, and there is pulse/blood pressure differential and widened mediastinum on CXR.
acute_pericarditis_idiopathic.clue: Chest pain that is sharp, pleuritic, and improves when leaning forward.

panic_attack_panic_disorder.hook: A panic attack causes chest pain from hyperventilation-induced coronary vasospasm and respiratory alkalosis, not from a one-way valve trapping air in the pleural space.
features: Acute chest pain with severe respiratory distress and diaphoresis—both can occur in panic, but the key is absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation, which are mechanical, not functional.
Tachypnea in panic is driven by anxiety and alkalosis; in tension pneumothorax it is a compensatory response to a collapsing lung and mediastinal shift.
Hypotension and distended neck veins in tension pneumothorax stem from impaired venous return due to increased intrathoracic pressure; panic does not cause obstructive shock.
traps: Aortic dissection: tearing pain radiating to back, pulse deficits, and often hypertension—not the silent chest and tracheal deviation of tension pneumothorax.
Pulmonary embolism: pleuritic pain, hypoxia, and sometimes hemoptysis—but no hyperresonance or absent breath sounds on one side.
Asthma exacerbation: diffuse wheezing and prolonged expiration, not unilateral absence of breath sounds with hyperresonance.
panic_attack_panic_disorder.clue: Unilateral absence of breath sounds with hyperresonance and tracheal deviation away from the affected side.

acute_coronary_syndrome_acs.hook: ACS is a plumbing problem in the coronary arteries; tension pneumothorax is a pressure problem in the pleural space—both cause chest pain but the mechanism of distress is entirely different.
features: Pleuristic chest pain with ipsilateral absent breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion—this is the hallmark of air trapping under tension, not myocardial ischemia.
Tracheal deviation away from the affected side and distended neck veins—these are physical exam findings of mediastinal shift and impaired venous return due to elevated intrapleural pressure.
Hypotension and pulsus paradoxus—these occur because the high pressure in the chest compresses the heart and great vessels, reducing cardiac output, a mechanism not seen in ACS.
traps: ACS: Pain is often substernal, pressure-like, radiating to the arm/jaw, with ST changes on ECG; no tracheal deviation or hyperresonance, and breath sounds are equal.
Pulmonary embolism: Presents with pleuritic pain and dyspnea but lacks hyperresonance, tracheal shift, and the 'silent chest' of tension pneumothorax; instead, there may be signs of DVT.
acute_coronary_syndrome_acs.clue: Sudden onset of severe respiratory distress with absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation—this is not a coronary event.

unstable_angina.hook: Unstable angina is a mismatch between myocardial oxygen demand and supply due to fixed or dynamic coronary obstruction, not a mechanical lung collapse.
features: Chest pain with exertion or at rest, often with ST depression or T-wave inversion on ECG due to subendocardial ischemia.
Pain is visceral, squeezing, or pressure-like, radiating to the jaw or left arm, driven by ischemic nociception.
No hemodynamic collapse or tracheal deviation because the pathology is in the coronary lumen, not the pleural space.
traps: Tension pneumothorax: Both cause acute chest pain and distress, but tension pneumothorax produces ipsilateral hyperresonance, tracheal deviation, and absent breath sounds due to air trapping in the pleural space—not myocardial ischemia.
Aortic dissection: Pain is tearing and radiates to the back, driven by intimal tear and false lumen, not by coronary supply-demand mismatch.
unstable_angina.clue: Unstable angina pain is reproducible with exertion and relieved by nitroglycerin, not positional or accompanied by tracheal deviation.

aortic_dissection_stanford_type_a.hook: Aortic dissection tears the intima, creating a false lumen that propagates under systemic pressure; tension pneumothorax traps air in the pleural space under positive pressure, collapsing the lung and shifting the mediastinum.
features: Ripping or tearing chest pain that may radiate to the back or neck, driven by the dissection flap extending along the aortic wall.
Pulse deficit or blood pressure differential between arms, caused by the false lumen compressing or occluding branch vessels.
Widened mediastinum on chest X-ray, reflecting the enlarged aortic silhouette from the contained hematoma.
traps: Tension pneumothorax: presents with hyperresonance and absent breath sounds on the affected side, not pulse deficits or back pain; the mechanism is air trapping under pressure, not intimal disruption.
Acute myocardial infarction: may cause tearing pain but lacks pulse deficits or mediastinal widening; pain is more substernal and pressure-like, driven by ischemia, not aortic wall dissection.
Pulmonary embolism: sudden dyspnea and pleuritic pain but no pulse deficits; mechanism is vascular occlusion by clot, not aortic wall tear.
aortic_dissection_stanford_type_a.clue: The presence of a blood pressure differential between arms or a pulse deficit strongly points to aortic dissection over tension pneumothorax.

atrial_fibrillation.hook: Air is trapped in the pleural space under pressure, collapsing the lung and shifting the mediastinum, which kinks the great veins and causes obstructive shock—this is not a primary cardiac or airway problem.
features: Acute chest pain with respiratory distress and hypotension: the tension physiology compresses the vena cava, reducing preload and cardiac output.
Tracheal deviation away from the affected side: the mediastinal shift is a physical exam sign of the pressure gradient across the mediastinum.
Absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on the affected side: air under tension does not allow lung expansion, and the trapped gas causes a tympanitic percussion note.
traps: Aortic dissection: presents with tearing chest pain and pulse deficits, but the mechanism is a tear in the aortic wall causing a false lumen, not a pleural air leak—no tracheal deviation or unilateral hyperresonance.

Pulmonary embolism: causes pleuritic chest pain and hypoxia from clot obstruction, but the mechanism is vascular occlusion, not air under pressure—no tracheal deviation and breath sounds are present unless infarction occurs.
Asthma exacerbation: causes wheezing and hyperinflation bilaterally due to bronchoconstriction, not unilateral air trapping—trachea is midline and breath sounds are present but prolonged expiration.
atrial_fibrillation.clue: Unilateral absent breath sounds with hyperresonance and tracheal deviation away from that side in a patient with acute respiratory distress.

acute_coronary_syndrome_acs_or_other_car.hook: Tension pneumothorax is a one-way valve mechanism where air enters the pleural space during inspiration but cannot exit, causing progressive mediastinal shift and obstructive shock.
features: Extreme respiratory distress with tracheal deviation away from the affected side and distended neck veins due to impaired venous return from mediastinal shift.
Hyperresonance to percussion and absent breath sounds on the affected side, with hypotension and tachycardia from reduced cardiac output.
Sudden onset of pleuritic chest pain after a precipitating event (e.g., trauma, mechanical ventilation, or spontaneous bleb rupture) with rapid deterioration.
traps: Cardiac tamponade: Both cause hypotension and distended neck veins, but tamponade has muffled heart sounds and equal breath sounds; tension pneumothorax has unilateral hyperresonance and tracheal deviation.
Massive pulmonary embolism: Presents with sudden dyspnea and hypotension, but lacks tracheal deviation and hyperresonance; ECG may show S1Q3T3, not electrical alternans.
Myocardial infarction: Can cause chest pain and diaphoresis, but does not produce unilateral absent breath sounds or tracheal shift; ECG shows ischemic changes.
acute_coronary_syndrome_acs_or_other_car.clue: Tracheal deviation away from the side of hyperresonance and absent breath sounds in a patient with sudden dyspnea and hypotension.
acute_coronary_syndrome_acs_or_other_car.diagnosis: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) or other cardiac conditions are the most likely diagnoses for a patient presenting with unknown chest pain

inferior_myocardial_infarction_stemi.hook: Inferior MI causes chest pain from acute myocardial ischemia due to occluded right coronary artery, but here the patient's severe respiratory distress and tracheal deviation point to tension pneumothorax—a mechanical compression of the heart and great vessels.
features: ST elevation in inferior leads (II, III, aVF) on ECG from transmural ischemia due to RCA occlusion.
Elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin) from myocardial necrosis.
Right ventricular involvement possible with hypotension and JVD from RV infarction.
traps: Tension pneumothorax: Tracheal deviation and absent breath sounds on one side, from air trapping causing mediastinal shift and impaired venous return, not coronary occlusion.
Pulmonary embolism: Pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea from acute right heart strain; ECG shows S1Q3T3, not inferior ST elevation.
Aortic dissection: Tearing chest pain radiating to back, with pulse deficit or widened mediastinum; no localized ST elevation on ECG.
inferior_myocardial_infarction_stemi.clue: Acute onset chest pain with severe respiratory distress and tracheal deviation away from the affected side on exam.

right_ventricular_myocardial_infarction.hook: Right ventricular infarction causes hypotension and JVD because the ischemic RV can't generate enough pressure to fill the LV, but here the tracheal deviation and hyperresonance point to tension pneumothorax compressing the entire mediastinum.
features: Hypotension with clear lungs and distended neck veins (Kussmaul sign) due to RV failure against high afterload from ischemia, not extrinsic compression.
ECG shows ST elevation in right-sided leads (V4R) and inferior leads, reflecting transmural ischemia of the thin RV free wall.
Elevated jugular venous pressure with a prominent y-descent (if in sinus rhythm) from impaired RV relaxation and filling.
traps: Tension pneumothorax also causes hypotension and JVD, but the mechanism is mediastinal shift compressing the SVC and RV—not RV ischemia—and tracheal deviation plus hyperresonance are absent in RV infarction.

Pulmonary embolism can mimic RV infarction with acute cor pulmonale and troponin elevation, but PE typically has a normal ECG or S1Q3T3 pattern, not inferior ST elevation, and is preceded by dyspnea, not chest pain.
right_ventricular_myocardial_infarction.clue: Tracheal deviation away from the side of decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance forces tension pneumothorax over RV infarction.

post_mi_pericarditis_dressler_syndrome.hook: Post-MI pericarditis is an inflammatory friction rub, not an air-trapping tension event — the mechanism is immune-mediated pericardial inflammation days to weeks after infarction, not acute gas trapping under pressure.
features: Pleuristic chest pain that worsens with inspiration or lying flat (pericardial inflammation stretches with movement).
Pericardial friction rub on auscultation (inflamed layers of pericardium create a scratchy sound).
Diffuse ST-segment elevation on ECG with PR depression (epicardial injury pattern, not localized to one vascular territory).
traps: Tension pneumothorax: both cause acute chest pain and dyspnea, but tension pneumothorax shows tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds, and hyperresonance on exam — the mechanism is air trapping in pleural space, not pericardial inflammation.
Pulmonary embolism: pleuritic pain and dyspnea overlap, but PE has sudden hypoxia, right heart strain, and no friction rub or diffuse ECG changes — mechanism is clot obstructing pulmonary arteries.

Aortic dissection: tearing chest pain and cardiovascular instability, but dissection produces pulse deficits, widened mediastinum, and no pericardial rub — mechanism is intimal tear with false lumen propagation.
post_mi_pericarditis_dressler_syndrome.clue: A respiratory distress case with absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation points to tension pneumothorax, not a friction rub or diffuse ECG changes.

subdural_hematoma.hook: In this elderly alcoholic with episodic altered mental status after a fall, the mechanism is venous bleeding from bridging veins torn by the brain lagging behind the skull during deceleration, slowly accumulating in the subdural space until mass effect impairs consciousness.
features: Episodic or fluctuating mental status due to gradual venous blood accumulation that intermittently decompresses into arachnoid granulations or is reabsorbed, temporarily relieving mass effect before reaccumulating.

History of recent fall (even minor) in an at-risk patient (elderly, alcoholic with cerebral atrophy) where stretched bridging veins are more vulnerable to shearing forces from brain movement relative to fixed dural sinuses.

Altered mental status without lateralizing signs early on, because the slow venous bleed initially compresses deep structures (thalamus, reticular activating system) rather than motor cortex or corticospinal tracts.
traps: Delirium from UTI or electrolyte disturbance: these cause global metabolic encephalopathy without focal signs, whereas subdural hematoma produces a progressive, often fluctuating course with eventual focal deficits or pupillary asymmetry due to uncal herniation.

Acute subarachnoid hemorrhage from ruptured aneurysm: that is arterial blood under high pressure causing sudden thunderclap headache and rapid loss of consciousness, not the gradual, stepwise decline seen with venous subdural bleeding.
subdural_hematoma.clue: Recent fall in an elderly patient with cerebral atrophy (from age or alcoholism) followed by fluctuating consciousness — the brain's shrinkage stretches bridging veins, making them prone to tear with even minor head deceleration.

bacterial_meningitis.hook: In subdural hematoma, altered mental status arises from venous bleeding that slowly accumulates in the subdural space, gradually compressing the brain—not from an infectious or inflammatory process like meningitis.
features: Recent fall with head trauma in an elderly alcoholic: brain atrophy stretches bridging veins, making them prone to tearing after even minor head trauma.
Episodic or fluctuating altered mental status: venous bleeding is slow, allowing the brain to compensate initially, leading to waxing and waning symptoms.
No fever, nuchal rigidity, or CSF pleocytosis: the absence of meningeal inflammation rules out bacterial meningitis.
traps: Bacterial meningitis: presents with acute fever, headache, and meningismus due to bacterial invasion of CSF, not from a mass effect or trauma; CSF shows elevated WBCs.
Metabolic encephalopathy (e.g., uremia, liver failure): lacks focal signs and history of head trauma; symptoms are diffuse and fluctuate without a triggering fall.
Stroke: ischemia or hemorrhage follows a vascular territory and is acute, not slowly progressive or episodic like a subdural hematoma.
bacterial_meningitis.clue: Recent fall in an elderly patient with alcoholism and episodic altered mental status, with no fever or neck stiffness.

urinary_tract_infection.hook: In an elderly alcoholic with altered mental status after a fall, a subdural hematoma is inevitable because the brain's movement relative to the skull shears bridging veins, which are already fragile from atrophy and coagulopathy.
features: Altered mental status that is episodic or fluctuating, reflecting intermittent mass effect or rebleeding from a venous bleed under low pressure.
History of chronic alcoholism causing brain atrophy and coagulopathy, which both increase the distance bridging veins must span and reduce their tensile strength.
Recent fall (even if minor) provides the kinetic force to shear those vulnerable bridging veins, leading to a slow accumulation of blood in the subdural space.
traps: UTI: Can cause altered mental status in the elderly but lacks the temporal link to head trauma (fall) and does not explain episodic fluctuations or focal neurological signs.
Metabolic encephalopathy: Would not be triggered by a fall and typically produces a global, non-fluctuating confusion without a history of head trauma.
urinary_tract_infection.clue: A clear history of a recent fall preceding the onset of altered mental status.

trauma.hook: In this elderly chronic alcoholic, the recent fall caused the brain to jolt relative to the skull, shearing bridging veins that drain from the cortex into the dural sinuses, leading to a slowly accumulating subdural hematoma that now compresses the brain and alters mental status.
features: Elderly brain atrophy stretches bridging veins, making them more vulnerable to tearing from even minor head acceleration-deceleration.
Chronic alcoholism causes cerebral atrophy (further stretching veins) and coagulopathy (impaired clotting), promoting ongoing venous oozing into the subdural space.
The episodic waxing-waning mental status reflects intermittent mass effect on the frontal/parietal cortex and possible seizure activity from cortical irritation.
traps: Delirium from UTI: systemic infection causes diffuse encephalopathy without focal brain compression or a clear temporal link to head trauma.
Metabolic encephalopathy (e.g., hypoglycemia or hyponatremia): produces global confusion but no space-occupying lesion and no history of head trauma.
trauma.clue: Episodic altered mental status that began immediately after a witnessed fall in an elderly patient.

electrolyte_disturbances.hook: In elderly with alcoholism, brain atrophy stretches bridging veins, making them prone to tear with minimal trauma—this is why a subdural hematoma, not an electrolyte disturbance, is the cause of altered mental status.
features: Recent fall with subsequent altered mental status—trauma triggers venous bleeding that accumulates slowly, unlike electrolyte shifts which are often gradual.
Episodic altered mental status—subdural hematoma can cause fluctuating consciousness as blood expands and compresses brain, whereas electrolyte disturbances usually cause persistent confusion.

History of chronic alcoholism—cerebral atrophy increases bridging vein tension, predisposing to subdural bleeding; alcohol also predisposes to electrolyte issues via poor nutrition, but the fall is the key event.
traps: Electrolyte disturbances—alcoholics often have hyponatremia or hypomagnesemia causing confusion, but these lack a preceding fall and do not cause episodic symptoms or focal signs.
Seizures—can cause altered mental status post-ictally, but seizure activity before fall is not described; subdural hematoma may itself trigger seizures, but the fall is the initiating event.
Bacterial meningitis—presents with fever, headache, and stiff neck; no trauma history and CSF analysis is diagnostic, not a CT finding of extra-axial blood.
electrolyte_disturbances.clue: A recent fall in an elderly alcoholic with episodic altered mental status is the trigger to image the head for subdural hematoma.

drug_or_alcohol_toxicity.hook: In this elderly alcoholic with episodic AMS after a fall, the mechanism is not pharmacologic neurodepression but a slowly accumulating venous bleed that progressively compresses the brain as the clot expands.
features: Episodic, waxing-waning confusion tied to a specific fall (not dose-dependent or substance clearance-related).
Chronic alcohol use causes brain atrophy, which stretches bridging veins and makes them more susceptible to shearing with minor trauma.
Focal neurological deficits or headache may be present, but the key is the temporal link to head trauma, not to ingestion or withdrawal.
traps: Alcohol intoxication: produces global CNS depression that improves with time and clearance, whereas SDH worsens or fluctuates without trauma recurrence.
Hepatic encephalopathy: causes asterixis and hyperammonemia, not focal signs or a direct temporal relationship to a fall.
drug_or_alcohol_toxicity.clue: Ask: 'Did the confusion start or worsen immediately after a fall?' – a positive answer favors structural bleed over toxicity.

heart_failure.hook: Heart failure causes altered mental status not by trauma but by cerebral hypoperfusion from low cardiac output and venous congestion from backward failure.
features: Altered mental status that is gradual and fluctuates with volume status, not episodic following a discrete fall
Physical exam findings of pulmonary edema (crackles), elevated JVD, and peripheral edema indicating fluid overload
Low cardiac output state with cool extremities, narrow pulse pressure, and possible hypotension
traps: Subdural hematoma: AMS is episodic with clear trauma history; exam may show focal deficits or no signs of volume overload; CT shows blood
Metabolic encephalopathy (e.g., uremia, hepatic): AMS may be similar but lacks heart failure signs; labs differentiate
Sepsis: Can have AMS and hypotension but typically fever, leukocytosis, and no signs of fluid overload
heart_failure.clue: Altered mental status after a fall in an elderly chronic alcoholic — always rule out subdural hematoma before attributing to heart failure.

metabolic.hook: This is a mass effect from venous bleeding, not a metabolic derangement—the patient's brain is being compressed, not poisoned.
features: Focal neurological deficits or asymmetric physical exam findings (e.g., unilateral weakness, pupillary asymmetry) that cannot be explained by a diffuse metabolic process.
Fluctuating level of consciousness with a clear temporal relationship to head trauma (recent fall) rather than a steady, progressive metabolic encephalopathy.
History of risk factors for bridging vein rupture: elderly (brain atrophy stretches veins) and chronic alcoholism (falls, coagulopathy, cerebral atrophy).
traps: Metabolic encephalopathy (e.g., from UTI, electrolyte disturbance, hepatic failure) is diffuse and symmetric, whereas subdural hematoma causes focal mass effect with lateralizing signs.
Intoxication or withdrawal (alcohol) can mimic altered mental status but lacks the focal findings and the acute-on-chronic temporal link to trauma.
Stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic) is typically sudden onset with maximal deficit at onset, while subdural hematoma often has a fluctuating or gradually worsening course over hours to days.
metabolic.clue: Any report of head trauma or fall in an elderly patient with altered mental status—especially if episodic or fluctuating—mandates a non-contrast head CT to rule out subdural hematoma.

normal_pressure_hydrocephalus.hook: When CSF absorption fails at the arachnoid granulations, it's a *communicating* hydrocephalus with a classic triad; when a bridging vein tears from brain-skull lag, it's a *subdural hematoma* with mass effect — both can cause gait and cognition changes, but the mechanism of the fluid collection is fundamentally different.
features: Gait apraxia (feet feel 'glued to the floor') due to stretching of periventricular corticospinal fibers from ventricular enlargement, not focal motor deficit.
Urinary urgency/incontinence from distortion of frontal micturition centers by dilated ventricles, not from cord compression.
Cognitive decline (subcortical dementia) with psychomotor slowing and apathy, stemming from disrupted frontal-subcortical circuits, not cortical damage.
traps: Subdural hematoma (the case diagnosis): both can cause frontal lobe signs and gait disturbance, but in SDH the mechanism is direct compression by a blood clot (venous bleeding) shifting the brain, not ventricular enlargement from impaired CSF resorption.

Alzheimer's disease: both cause cognitive decline, but NPH has a *subcortical* pattern (slow processing, apathy) with gait and bladder changes, while Alzheimer's is *cortical* (amnesia, aphasia, apraxia) and lacks the classic gait triad.

Parkinson's disease: both have gait difficulty and bradykinesia, but NPH lacks tremor, rigidity, and response to levodopa; the gait in NPH is 'magnetic' (feet stuck to floor) vs parkinsonian shuffling.
normal_pressure_hydrocephalus.clue: A gait that looks like the feet are 'glued to the floor' (magnetic gait) with impaired heel-to-toe walking, in a patient with ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy on imaging.

transient_ischemic_attack_tia.hook: A TIA is a transient episode of focal neurological dysfunction due to ischemia, not the diffuse, persistent encephalopathy from a subdural hematoma's mass effect on the brain.
features: Focal symptoms (e.g., unilateral weakness, speech difficulty) that resolve completely within minutes to hours, not global confusion
Symptoms are vascular-territory specific, not related to position or recent head trauma
No progressive or waxing-waning level of consciousness; TIA patients are typically alert and oriented between episodes
traps: Migraine aura: aura develops gradually (over minutes), often with visual phenomena, and is followed by headache; TIA is sudden, headache is not a feature
Seizure: seizure can cause transient focal deficits (Todd's paresis) but is typically followed by postictal confusion, not a lucid interval, and may have tonic-clonic activity
Hypoglycemia: can mimic any stroke-like symptom but is global (not focal) and resolves with glucose administration; check glucose first
transient_ischemic_attack_tia.clue: The patient's altered mental status is persistent and progressive after a fall, not transient and focal—this points to a structural lesion like subdural hematoma, not a vascular ischemic event.

grand_mal_seizure_generalized_tonic_clon.hook: In an elderly alcoholic with falls, episodic altered mental status is not seizure but the brain's venous bridge veins tearing—bleeding into the subdural space compresses cortex, not a cortical electrical storm.
features: Altered mental status that fluctuates (lucid intervals) as venous blood accumulates and tamponades, mimicking postictal confusion but without convulsive or EEG correlate.
Focal neurological deficits (e.g., hemiparesis, anisocoria) from mass effect on motor/sensory cortex, not the generalized symmetric motor activity of a tonic-clonic seizure.
Headache and progressive drowsiness from rising intracranial pressure due to slow venous bleed, unlike the abrupt loss of consciousness followed by rapid recovery in a seizure.
traps: Postictal confusion: In seizure, confusion follows a convulsive event and resolves over minutes to hours; here, confusion waxes and wanes without a preceding convulsion, driven by intermittent brain compression.
Delirium tremens: Alcohol withdrawal causes autonomic hyperactivity and visual hallucinations, but not the focal signs or stepwise decline from a space-occupying lesion.
Transient ischemic attack: Focal deficits in TIA resolve completely within 24 hours and lack the progressive, mass-effect-driven drowsiness seen with subdural hematoma.
grand_mal_seizure_generalized_tonic_clon.clue: A lucid interval after fall, then fluctuating consciousness with focal neurologic signs (e.g., unilateral weakness, dilated pupil) in a patient at risk for brain atrophy (elderly, alcoholic).

septic_shock.hook: In septic shock, altered mental status is driven by systemic vasodilation and hypoperfusion of the brain due to distributive shock, not by a focal mass effect compressing cerebral tissue.
features: Warm, flushed skin from peripheral vasodilation (early septic shock) vs. the focal neurological deficits seen with subdural hematoma.
Fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, and tachypnea reflecting a systemic inflammatory response, absent in subdural hematoma unless concurrent infection.
Hypotension that is poorly responsive to volume resuscitation, due to cytokine-mediated vasoplegia, not explained by a space-occupying lesion.
traps: Meningitis: Both cause altered mental status and fever, but meningitis presents with nuchal rigidity and photophobia from meningeal inflammation, whereas septic shock lacks focal signs and has profound hypotension.
Delirium from UTI: Common in elderly, but septic shock has hemodynamic instability (lactate >2, need for vasopressors) not typical of simple UTI.
septic_shock.clue: Look for hypotension and fever with a source (e.g., pneumonia, UTI) in the setting of altered mental status, not a history of head trauma or focal deficits.

endometrioma.hook: Endometrioma is not just a cyst—it's a chronic, ectopic endometrial implant that bleeds cyclically, leading to a 'chocolate cyst' with dense adhesions that cause pain on stretch during intercourse.
features: Severe, cyclic pelvic pain that worsens with sexual activity due to traction on adhesed ovarian tissue
Localized right adnexal mass in a reproductive-age woman with a history of dysmenorrhea
Ultrasound shows a homogeneous, low-level echogenic ('ground glass') cyst, reflecting old blood from repeated hemorrhage
traps: Ectopic pregnancy: presents with acute pain and adnexal mass but with amenorrhea and positive β-hCG; no cyclic pattern or chronic dysmenorrhea
Tubo-ovarian abscess: fever, elevated WBC, and purulent discharge; pain is constant and infectious, not cyclic or triggered by menses
endometrioma.clue: Pelvic pain that is severe and specifically worsens with sexual activity (dyspareunia) in a reproductive-age woman with a right adnexal mass.

there_is_a_large_differential_for_a_righ.hook: Endometriomas are functional cysts formed by ectopic endometrial tissue that bleeds cyclically, creating a 'chocolate cyst' that expands and ruptures with hormonal surges.
features: Cyclic exacerbation: Pain worsens with menstruation and sexual activity due to hormonal stimulation of ectopic endometrium causing local inflammation and distension.
Localized tenderness: Pain is typically unilateral (right adnexal) as the cyst distorts the ovary and stretches its capsule during the luteal phase.
Ultrasound findings: A unilocular, ground-glass echogenic cyst without internal vascularity, reflecting old blood products within the endometrioma.
traps: Ectopic pregnancy: Presents with adnexal mass and pain, but has amenorrhea, positive β-hCG, and often unilateral sharp pain with vaginal bleeding—no cyclic pattern.

Tubo-ovarian abscess: Causes adnexal pain and mass, but is associated with fever, elevated WBC, and cervical motion tenderness; ultrasound shows complex, thick-walled, fluid-filled structure with debris.
Ovarian torsion: Acute severe pain with nausea/vomiting, but lacks cyclic exacerbation and ultrasound shows enlarged ovary with absent arterial Doppler flow.
there_is_a_large_differential_for_a_righ.clue: Pain that is consistently worse during menses and with intercourse (dyspareunia) points to endometrioma rather than other adnexal masses.
there_is_a_large_differential_for_a_righ.diagnosis: There is a large differential for a right adnexal mass in a reproductive age female. This could include ectopic pregnancy

tuboovarian_abscess.hook: A tuboovarian abscess is an infectious collection in the adnexa that extends from the fallopian tube into the ovary, causing a complex mass with surrounding inflammation, distinct from a hemorrhagic endometrioma which is a sterile, blood-filled cyst from endometrial tissue.
features: Fever and leukocytosis are typical due to active infection, while endometrioma usually lacks systemic signs.
Unilateral or bilateral complex adnexal mass with thick walls, internal debris, and surrounding fat stranding on imaging, whereas endometrioma appears as a homogeneous, ground-glass echogenic cyst.
Marked tenderness on pelvic exam and cervical motion tenderness (chandelier sign) from peritoneal irritation, which is less prominent in endometrioma unless ruptured.
traps: Ruptured endometrioma: Both cause acute pelvic pain and a complex mass, but endometrioma lacks fever and purulent discharge; imaging shows layering debris without gas or abscess wall enhancement.
Ectopic pregnancy: Both present with adnexal mass and pain, but ectopic has positive β-hCG and no systemic infection signs.
Ovarian neoplasm: Can mimic a complex mass, but lacks acute infectious symptoms and has different imaging features (e.g., solid components, papillary projections).
tuboovarian_abscess.clue: The presence of fever and purulent cervical discharge in a patient with an adnexal mass strongly points to tuboovarian abscess rather than endometrioma.

inflammatory_bowel_disease.hook: In IBD, pelvic pain arises from transmural inflammation causing fistulous tracts or abscesses that irritate the adnexa, not from cyclic hormonal stimulation of ectopic endometrium.
features: Pain that is often colicky or associated with diarrhea, tenesmus, or bloody stools, reflecting mucosal and transmural inflammation.
Fever, leukocytosis, or elevated CRP due to active inflammatory process, not typically present in endometrioma.
Radiologic findings of bowel wall thickening, mucosal enhancement, or fistulous communication on CT/MRI, unlike the cystic, hemorrhagic adnexal mass of endometrioma.
traps: Endometrioma: pain is cyclical, linked to menses, and due to ectopic endometrial tissue causing local inflammation and adhesions, not transmural bowel inflammation.
Tubo-ovarian abscess: pain is acute, severe, with fever and elevated WBCs, but arises from ascending infection, not chronic bowel inflammation.
Ovarian mass: pain is often dull or pressure-related from mass effect, not associated with gastrointestinal symptoms or systemic inflammation.
inflammatory_bowel_disease.clue: Presence of chronic diarrhea or hematochezia accompanying the pelvic pain strongly points to IBD rather than endometrioma.

ovarian_mass.hook: Endometriomas are 'chocolate cysts' arising from ectopic endometrial tissue that bleeds cyclically, causing an encapsulated, painful mass that distorts the adnexal anatomy.
features: Severe, cyclic pelvic pain that worsens with sexual activity (dyspareunia) due to inflammation and traction on the peritoneum and surrounding structures from the expanding hemorrhagic cyst.
Localized right adnexal mass on exam or imaging, often with a characteristic 'ground glass' echogenicity on ultrasound from old blood products.
Pain that correlates with menstrual cycle phase, as ectopic endometrial tissue responds to hormonal stimulation, leading to cyclic bleeding and inflammation within the cyst wall.
traps: Ectopic pregnancy: presents with adnexal pain and mass, but mechanism involves implantation of fertilized ovum in fallopian tube, not cyclic endometrial bleeding; β-hCG positive differentiates.
Tubo-ovarian abscess: adnexal mass and pain, but mechanism is infectious with fever, purulent discharge, and elevated WBC; not cyclic or hormonally driven.
Hemorrhagic ovarian cyst: also has sudden pain and internal echoes on ultrasound, but lacks the chronic cyclic pattern and dense adhesions of endometrioma; resolves spontaneously.
ovarian_mass.clue: Pelvic pain that is consistently worse with menses or sexual activity, with a fixed, tender adnexal mass on bimanual exam.

theca.hook: In endometrioma, the pain is caused by cyclic bleeding into a fixed, fibrotic cyst that stretches the peritoneum, whereas theca lutein cysts are hormonally driven and painless unless they rupture or torse.
features: Pain that worsens with sexual activity (due to direct mechanical stretching of the adherent, fibrotic cyst wall).
Right adnexal mass with a history of cyclic pain (endometrioma bleeds each cycle, expanding the cyst).
Fixed, tender adnexal mass on exam (fibrotic adhesions tether the cyst to surrounding structures).
traps: Hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst: also bleeds internally but is not fibrotic; pain is acute from rupture, not progressive and sex-related.
Tubo-ovarian abscess: pain from infection, not cyclic; fever and leukocytosis differentiate.
Ovarian torsion: acute, severe, non-positional pain with nausea/vomiting; not specifically worsened by intercourse.
theca.clue: Severe pelvic pain that worsens with sexual activity in a reproductive-age woman with a right adnexal mass.

pelvic_inflammatory_disease.hook: Pelvic inflammatory disease is an ascending infection causing tubal inflammation and adhesions, whereas an endometrioma is a functional cyst of ectopic endometrial tissue that bleeds cyclically and causes pain via local irritation and mass effect.
features: PID pain is typically bilateral, diffuse, and associated with cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, and mucopurulent discharge due to inflammation of the fallopian tubes and peritoneum.
PID often presents with fever, elevated WBC, and can have an elevated ESR/CRP due to an active infectious process.
PID may be associated with recent sexual activity, multiple partners, or an STI history, whereas endometrioma pain is cyclic and linked to menses.
traps: Endometrioma can mimic PID with unilateral adnexal pain and dyspareunia, but its pain is cyclic and lacks systemic inflammatory signs.
Ruptured ovarian cyst or ectopic pregnancy can cause acute pelvic pain; however, ectopic pregnancy will have +beta-hCG and possible adnexal mass, while PID has no pregnancy and signs of infection.
Tubo-ovarian abscess is a complication of PID that can present as a complex adnexal mass, but it is associated with fever and leukocytosis, unlike an uncomplicated endometrioma.
pelvic_inflammatory_disease.clue: Pain that is unilateral, cyclic, and worse with menses, with no fever or cervical motion tenderness, strongly suggests endometrioma rather than PID.

ovarian_torsion.hook: Ovarian torsion is a vascular emergency where the adnexa twists on its pedicle, causing venous occlusion and hemorrhagic infarction before arterial compromise—unlike endometrioma, which is a functional cyst filled with old blood causing pain via cyclic rupture and local inflammation.
features: Sudden, severe, unilateral pelvic pain that may be colicky or constant, often with nausea/vomiting due to peritoneal irritation from ischemia.
Pain may wax and wane as the ovary partially twists and untwists, but unlike endometrioma, it is not necessarily linked to menses or sexual activity.
Ultrasound shows an enlarged, edematous ovary with peripheral follicles ('string of pearls') and absent or reversed arterial/venous Doppler flow.
traps: Endometrioma: pain is typically cyclic, related to menses, and dyspareunia is classic; ultrasound shows a cystic mass with ground-glass echogenicity, not an enlarged ovary with absent flow.
Ruptured hemorrhagic cyst: presents with acute pain but is often associated with a cyst on ultrasound and lacks the vascular compromise signs of torsion.
ovarian_torsion.clue: In a reproductive-age woman with acute, severe unilateral pelvic pain and nausea/vomiting, the presence of an enlarged ovary with absent venous Doppler flow on ultrasound is pathognomonic for torsion.

diabetic_ketoacidosis.hook: In DKA, abdominal pain and vomiting arise from the metabolic acidosis itself—ketoacids stimulate the chemoreceptor trigger zone and cause gastric ileus, not from a primary intra-abdominal pathology.
features: Diffuse abdominal pain without peritonitis or guarding, driven by acidosis-induced gastric stasis and mesenteric ischemia.
Lethargy and vomiting from intracellular dehydration and ketosis, with compensatory Kussmaul respirations (not just hyperventilation).
Hyperglycemia with profound osmotic diuresis leading to total body potassium depletion, despite a potentially normal or high serum K+ on initial labs due to acidemia shifting K+ extracellularly.
traps: Acute abdomen (e.g., appendicitis, pancreatitis) – DKA pain is diffuse without rebound/rigidity; acidosis resolves pain, whereas surgical causes persist.
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) – HHS lacks significant ketosis and acidosis; mental status changes are from hyperosmolality, not acidemia, and abdominal pain is far less prominent.
Gastroenteritis – DKA vomiting is driven by acidosis, not gut infection; the presence of hyperglycemia, ketonuria, and wide anion gap metabolic acidosis distinguishes it.
diabetic_ketoacidosis.clue: Look for Kussmaul breathing (deep, rapid respirations) and a fruity acetone odor on the breath—these are the bedside signs of the metabolic acidosis driving abdominal symptoms in DKA.

intra_abdominal_abscess_post_appendectom.hook: This patient's diffuse abdominal pain, vomiting, and lethargy in the setting of extreme hyperglycemia are driven by DKA's osmotic diuresis and ketone-induced metabolic acidosis, not by a localized peritoneal collection.
features: Diffuse, non-localized abdominal pain from gastric stasis and ileus caused by hypokalemia and acidosis, not from peritoneal inflammation.
Vomiting and lethargy secondary to severe metabolic acidosis and hyperosmolality, not from a septic focus.
Elevated glucose and anion gap metabolic acidosis with ketonuria, confirming DKA as the root cause of the abdominal symptoms.
traps: Acute appendicitis: Pain typically localizes to RLQ with peritoneal signs (rebound, guarding) and fever, whereas DKA pain is diffuse and without true peritonitis.

Intra-abdominal abscess: Presents with persistent fever, localized tenderness, and a history of surgery (e.g., post-appendectomy); DKA lacks a surgical history and the pain resolves with metabolic correction.
intra_abdominal_abscess_post_appendectom.clue: Abdominal pain that resolves with insulin and fluid resuscitation, without peritoneal signs, points to DKA rather than a surgical abdomen.

hepatitis_a_with_aspiration_pneumonia.hook: DKA causes abdominal pain via metabolic acidosis triggering gastric ileus and visceral inflammation, not via hepatocyte necrosis or foreign-body airway inflammation.
features: Diffuse abdominal pain from acidosis-induced gastroparesis and ileus, not right-upper-quadrant tenderness of hepatitis.
Lethargy from hyperosmolality and ketosis, not hepatic encephalopathy or aspiration-related hypoxia.
Vomiting from ketoacidosis-driven nausea, not from hepatitis A prodrome or aspiration pneumonitis.
traps: Hepatitis A: abdominal pain is RUQ from liver capsule stretch (hepatocyte necrosis), not diffuse; plus jaundice and transaminitis—absent in DKA.
Aspiration pneumonia: respiratory distress with focal crackles after vomiting—here vomiting is cause, not consequence; no aspiration event or pulmonary findings.
hepatitis_a_with_aspiration_pneumonia.clue: Polydipsia, polyuria, and weight loss precede the abdominal pain, pointing to new-onset diabetes rather than infection.

acute_gastritis_nsaid_induced.hook: In DKA, abdominal pain is not from gastric mucosal injury but from metabolic acidosis-induced gastric atony and mesenteric ischemia.
features: Diffuse, poorly localized abdominal pain without epigastric dominance, worsened by acidosis severity
Nausea/vomiting due to delayed gastric emptying from acidotic inhibition of smooth muscle contraction
Pain resolves with correction of acidosis, not with antacids or PPI therapy
traps: Acute gastritis/peptic ulcer disease: pain is epigastric, burning, often relieved by food/antacids, and triggered by NSAIDs or H. pylori, not by hyperglycemia or acidosis
Pancreatitis: pain is epigastric radiating to back, with elevated lipase, not explained by anion gap acidosis alone
Gastroenteritis: pain is crampy, often with diarrhea, and not tied to acid-base status or hyperglycemia
acute_gastritis_nsaid_induced.clue: Abdominal pain that improves as the anion gap closes during insulin therapy.

acute_diverticulitis_complicated_with_sm.hook: The diffuse abdominal pain and vomiting in this young woman are driven by the osmotic diuresis and volume depletion from severe hyperglycemia, not by focal inflammation.
features: Diffuse, non-localized abdominal pain with vomiting and lethargy, consistent with metabolic acidosis and electrolyte shifts rather than peritoneal irritation.
History of polyuria and polydipsia (implicit from new-onset diabetes) causing volume contraction, which worsens acidosis and pain.
Elevated glucose (>600) and anion gap metabolic acidosis, mechanistically explaining abdominal pain via gastric stasis and acidosis-induced visceral discomfort.
traps: Acute diverticulitis typically presents with focal left lower quadrant pain and fever, driven by localized colonic inflammation; DKA causes diffuse pain from metabolic derangement.
Gastroenteritis may mimic DKA with vomiting and pain, but DKA lacks infectious diarrhea and has hallmark hyperglycemia and ketosis.
Pancreatitis can cause epigastric pain and vomiting, but DKA pain is diffuse and resolves with metabolic correction, not correlated with lipase elevation.
acute_diverticulitis_complicated_with_sm.clue: Diffuse abdominal pain in a young woman with polyuria, polydipsia, and no focal tenderness on exam.

irritable_bowel_syndrome.hook: In IBS, pain arises from visceral hypersensitivity and altered brain-gut signaling, not from metabolic acidosis or volume depletion as in DKA.
features: Pain that is crampy, relieved with defecation, and associated with altered stool frequency or form (Rome IV criteria).
Symptoms are chronic (>6 months) and triggered by stress, meals, or specific foods (gut-brain axis dysregulation).
No systemic signs like fever, tachycardia, or altered mental status (absence of inflammation or metabolic derangement).
traps: DKA: Abdominal pain is due to gastric stasis and acidosis-induced mucosal irritation, but key differentiating features are polydipsia, polyuria, Kussmaul breathing, and hyperglycemia with anion gap acidosis.
Gastroenteritis: Infectious cause with acute onset, fever, and positive stool studies; IBS lacks inflammatory markers and has a relapsing-remitting course.
irritable_bowel_syndrome.clue: Pain is chronic, associated with bowel movements, and lacks the vital sign instability or metabolic acidosis seen in this young woman with DKA.

acute_cholecystitis.hook: Right upper quadrant pain in DKA is not from gallstones but from the hepatobiliary system drowning in ketones and fatty acids.
features: Nausea and vomiting as a result of metabolic acidosis and ketone accumulation irritating the GI tract.
Diffuse abdominal pain from gastric distention and hepatic capsule stretch due to fatty liver infiltration, not localized peritonitis.
Lethargy and altered mental status driven by hyperosmolarity and acidosis, not sepsis or biliary obstruction.
traps: Acute cholecystitis: pain is localized to RUQ with Murphy's sign, fever, and leukocytosis, whereas DKA pain is diffuse and driven by metabolic derangement.
Pancreatitis: epigastric pain with radiation to back and elevated lipase, while DKA has diffuse pain and elevated glucose/ketones as primary drivers.
Appendicitis: pain migrates to RLQ with peritoneal signs, unlike the vague, diffuse pain of DKA.
acute_cholecystitis.clue: A young patient with diffuse abdominal pain, vomiting, and lethargy plus a history of polydipsia and weight loss should prompt immediate fingerstick glucose and serum ketone measurement.

glucose_6_phosphate_dehydrogenase_g6pd_d.hook: In DKA, the abdominal pain and vomiting are driven by ketone-mediated gastric stasis and metabolic acidosis, not by red cell lysis from oxidative stress.
features: Hemolysis from G6PD deficiency causes acute hemoglobinuria (dark urine) and indirect hyperbilirubinemia, not ketonuria or high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
Abdominal pain in G6PD hemolysis is due to acute splenic congestion from sequestered damaged red cells, whereas in DKA it stems from gastric irritation and ileus.
Lethargy in G6PD crisis is from acute anemia and tissue hypoxia, contrasting with DKA where lethargy results from hyperosmolality, acidosis, and ketone-induced CNS depression.
traps: DKA: Abdominal pain + vomiting + lethargy mimics an acute abdomen or hemolytic crisis, but the key differentiator is hyperglycemia, ketonuria, and high anion gap acidosis without evidence of hemolysis (normal LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin).
Acute pancreatitis: Can present with epigastric pain and vomiting, but lacks the oxidative trigger (e.g., fava beans, sulfa drugs) and hemoglobinuria seen in G6PD hemolysis.
glucose_6_phosphate_dehydrogenase_g6pd_d.clue: Check urine dipstick for blood without RBCs on microscopy (hemoglobinuria) and review medication/dietary history for oxidative triggers.

intussusception.hook: In DKA, the bowel is paralyzed by hypokalemia and acidosis, not obstructed by a mechanical lead point.
features: Diffuse, crampy pain without focal tenderness or peritoneal signs—visceral autonomic neuropathy from acidosis/hypokalemia.
Vomiting and anorexia are driven by ketone-mediated chemoreceptor trigger zone activation, not by proximal bowel obstruction.
Abdominal distension and diminished bowel sounds reflect ileus from electrolyte derangement, not mechanical blockage.
traps: Acute appendicitis: focal RLQ pain with guarding—here the pain is diffuse and exam is benign because the peritoneum is not inflamed.
Intussusception: colicky pain with currant jelly stool—here pain is constant and vomiting precedes any bloody output because the mechanism is metabolic, not structural.
Gastroenteritis: watery diarrhea is common—here constipation or obstipation is typical because hypokalemia inhibits peristalsis.
intussusception.clue: Polydipsia and polyuria predating the abdominal pain, with a serum glucose >600 mg/dL and an anion gap >20.

nephrolithiasis_kidney_stone.hook: In DKA, abdominal pain is driven by visceral acidosis and volume depletion, not by an obstructing stone.
features: Diffuse, non-colicky pain without radiation to the groin
Pain accompanied by vomiting, lethargy, and Kussmaul respirations (compensatory tachypnea)
Anion gap metabolic acidosis with ketonemia and hyperglycemia (glucose >600 mg/dL)
traps: Acute abdomen mimics (e.g., appendicitis, pancreatitis) — but DKA pain is bilateral and resolves with acidosis correction
Nephrolithiasis — colicky, unilateral flank pain with hematuria, not diffuse and not associated with high anion gap acidosis
nephrolithiasis_kidney_stone.clue: The presence of Kussmaul respirations and a fruity odor on the breath points to DKA over a surgical abdomen.

lead_intoxication_with_encephalopathy.hook: Abdominal pain + lethargy + vomiting in a young patient without diabetes history could be DKA, but the actual mechanism here is lead inhibiting ALAD and ferrochelatase, causing neurotoxicity and colic via disrupted heme synthesis and direct smooth muscle effects.
features: Lead causes abdominal colic by interfering with smooth muscle contraction via heme pathway disruption and direct toxic effects on autonomic ganglia.
Encephalopathy results from lead-induced capillary damage and increased blood-brain barrier permeability, compounded by inhibition of mitochondrial enzymes.
Anemia (microcytic/hypochromic) from impaired heme synthesis due to ferrochelatase and ALAD inhibition, with basophilic stippling on smear.
traps: DKA: abdominal pain from acidosis and electrolyte shifts, but DKA has hyperglycemia, ketosis, and anion gap metabolic acidosis—lead does not.

Acute porphyria: shares abdominal pain and neuropsychiatric symptoms due to heme pathway dysregulation, but porphyria involves accumulation of porphyrin precursors, not lead; lead specifically inhibits ALAD and ferrochelatase, causing increased ALA and coproporphyrin in urine.
Guillain-Barre: can cause ascending paralysis, but lead neuropathy is motor-predominant with wrist drop and no sensory loss typical of GBS.
lead_intoxication_with_encephalopathy.clue: Look for lead exposure history (pica, occupational, old paint) and basophilic stippling on peripheral smear, plus elevated blood lead level—none of which occur in DKA.

acute_bacterial_gastroenteritis.hook: This patient’s abdominal pain and vomiting are driven by metabolic acidosis from ketone accumulation, not by mucosal inflammation or infection.
features: Diffuse abdominal pain without fever, tenesmus, or bloody stools—consistent with visceral irritation from acidosis, not direct bowel wall invasion.
Vomiting and lethargy out of proportion to GI symptoms, driven by compensatory hyperventilation and cerebral effects of ketoacidosis.
Polyuria and polydipsia in the HPI are the key mechanistic clues: osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia, not from infectious enteritis.
traps: Acute gastroenteritis: causes vomiting and abdominal pain but typically with fever, diarrhea, and no profound dehydration or acidemia; anion gap is normal.
Appendicitis: pain localizes to RLQ with peritoneal signs, not diffuse; vomiting is secondary to pain, not primary metabolic drive; no hyperglycemia or ketosis.
Pancreatitis: epigastric pain radiating to back, elevated lipase, and often normal glucose and anion gap unless severe.
acute_bacterial_gastroenteritis.clue: Deep, rapid breathing (Kussmaul respirations) on exam in a patient with diffuse abdominal pain and vomiting—this is the compensatory sigh of metabolic acidosis, not a GI primary process.

acute_abdomen_undetermined_etiology.hook: The diffuse abdominal pain here is a direct consequence of metabolic acidosis triggering visceral stretch receptors and impaired gut perfusion, not a primary intra-abdominal catastrophe.
features: Diffuse, non-localized pain without peritoneal signs—consistent with acidosis-driven gastric stasis and ileus rather than focal inflammation.
Concurrent lethargy and vomiting suggesting systemic metabolic derangement (ketosis, hyperosmolality) causing neuronal dysfunction and fluid losses.
Tachycardia and tachypnea as compensatory mechanisms for hypovolemia and metabolic acidosis, producing Kussmaul respirations that can mimic respiratory distress.
traps: Acute pancreatitis: epigastric pain with vomiting; but in DKA, lipase may be mildly elevated due to ketosis, and the pain is diffuse and resolves with acidosis correction—not a primary pancreatic process.
Appendicitis: RLQ pain; here pain is diffuse, without focal tenderness or guarding, and the systemic symptoms (lethargy, vomiting) precede the pain pattern.

Gastroenteritis: infectious diarrhea and cramps; but DKA presents with polyuria and polydipsia prior to vomiting, and the anion gap metabolic acidosis is disproportionately severe relative to GI losses alone.
acute_abdomen_undetermined_etiology.clue: A 'fruity' odor on the breath (acetone) or a history of polyuria and polydipsia preceding the abdominal pain should immediately prompt a fingerstick glucose and serum ketone measurement.

ischemic_colitis.hook: In DKA, the bowel suffers a low-flow state from hypovolemia and acidosis, but ischemic colitis requires a vascular territory occlusion or prolonged hypotension—a different mechanism that DKA alone rarely triggers.
features: Pain is typically left-sided or periumbilical, reflecting watershed zones of the splenic flexure and rectosigmoid (superior/inferior mesenteric artery border), unlike DKA's diffuse, crampy pain from gastric stasis.
Hematochezia or bloody diarrhea appears early, driven by mucosal necrosis and reperfusion injury, whereas DKA vomiting is non-bloody and due to ketone-driven nausea.
Distention, tenderness, and peritoneal signs emerge if transmural ischemia progresses, contrasting with DKA's soft, non-peritoneal abdomen unless severe acidosis causes ileus.
traps: DKA can mimic ischemic colitis with abdominal pain and lactic acidosis; but DKA's lactate rises from ketone metabolism and hypoperfusion globally, not from localized bowel necrosis, and resolves with insulin/fluids.

Infectious colitis (e.g., C. diff) causes bloody diarrhea and pain, but lacks the vascular watershed pattern and has fever, recent antibiotics, or stool toxin positivity, not the low-flow trigger of ischemia.
ischemic_colitis.clue: Blood per rectum or guaiac-positive stool in the setting of hypotension or vasopressor use, not just hyperglycemia and acidosis.

ulcerative_colitis.hook: The abdominal pain and vomiting in DKA aren't from gut inflammation—they're from the osmotic diuresis and volume depletion causing mesenteric ischemia and gastric stasis.
features: Diffuse, non-colicky abdominal pain without peritoneal signs, arising from splanchnic hypoperfusion due to profound volume loss.
Nausea and vomiting driven by gastric atony and delayed emptying from electrolyte disturbances and acidosis.
Kussmaul respirations (compensatory hyperventilation) often misinterpreted as respiratory distress, but are a direct response to metabolic acidosis.
traps: Acute abdomen (e.g., appendicitis, pancreatitis) – DKA pain is vague and positional, without rebound or guarding; amylase may be mildly elevated but lipase normal.
Gastroenteritis – vomiting and pain are present, but DKA has polyuria, polydipsia, and fruity breath (acetone) absent in infectious causes.
Sepsis – fever and leukocytosis can occur in DKA from stress response; blood cultures and lactate help differentiate.
ulcerative_colitis.clue: Anion gap metabolic acidosis with elevated glucose >250 mg/dL and ketones in the setting of abdominal pain and vomiting.

hemoperitoneum_from_ruptured_ovarian_cys.hook: In DKA, the abdominal pain is driven by metabolic acidosis causing gastric ileus and peritoneal irritation via ketone-induced inflammation, not by intraperitoneal blood.
features: Diffuse, crampy abdominal pain with nausea/vomiting due to gastric stasis from acidosis and electrolyte shifts
Kussmaul breathing (compensatory respiratory alkalosis) and fruity breath odor from ketone accumulation
Lethargy and altered mental status from hyperosmolality and acidosis, not hypovolemic shock
traps: Hemoperitoneum from ruptured ovarian cyst: pain is more focal, sudden, and associated with orthostatic hypotension from blood loss; no Kussmaul breathing or hyperglycemia
Acute pancreatitis: epigastric pain radiating to back, often with elevated lipase; no hyperglycemic extremes or anion gap acidosis from ketones
hemoperitoneum_from_ruptured_ovarian_cys.clue: In DKA, abdominal pain improves with insulin and fluid resuscitation as acidosis resolves, whereas surgical causes worsen or remain constant.

acute_abdomen_non_specific.hook: DKA doesn't cause an acute abdomen; the acute abdomen is a metabolic illusion from ketoacidosis-driven gastric ileus and visceral acidosis.
features: Diffuse, poorly-localized abdominal pain without rebound or guarding—visceral irritation from acidosis, not peritoneal inflammation.
Lethargy and vomiting out of proportion to abdominal findings—systemic metabolic encephalopathy and acid-base disturbance.
Tachypnea with deep, sighing respirations (Kussmaul)—compensatory respiratory alkalosis trying to blow off CO2 to correct metabolic acidosis.
traps: Appendicitis or cholecystitis: These cause focal, progressive pain with peritonitis. DKA pain is diffuse, non-progressive, and resolves with metabolic correction.
Pancreatitis: Can also cause epigastric pain and vomiting, but amylase/lipase are elevated and pain is more severe and persistent despite DKA treatment.
acute_abdomen_non_specific.clue: Blood glucose > 500 mg/dL with positive serum ketones and an elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis in a patient with diffuse abdominal pain and no peritoneal signs.

acute_abdomen_unspecified_etiology.hook: Her diffuse abdominal pain, vomiting, and lethargy are driven by a metabolic acidosis that directly irritates the peritoneum and stimulates chemoreceptor trigger zone—not by a surgical intra-abdominal catastrophe.
features: Diffuse, non-localized pain with vomiting and lethargy—consistent with acidosis-driven nausea and ileus, not focal inflammation.
Kussmaul breathing (compensatory tachypnea) would be triggered by the anion gap acidosis, providing a physical sign absent in surgical peritonitis.
Severe hyperglycemia (glucose >600) with volume depletion causes osmotic diuresis and intracellular dehydration, worsening lethargy and pain perception.
traps: Acute appendicitis or pancreatitis: pain in DKA is diffuse, not migrating or epigastric; vomiting is metabolic, not obstructive; and fever is absent unless infection triggered DKA.
Gastroenteritis: DKA produces profound volume loss and altered mental status out of proportion to stool output, with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
Surgical abdomen: rebound and guarding are absent because pain is visceral from acidosis, not from parietal peritoneal inflammation.
acute_abdomen_unspecified_etiology.clue: A high anion gap metabolic acidosis with hyperglycemia and ketonuria in a patient with diffuse abdominal pain and lethargy.

west_nile_encephalitis.hook: This is a flavivirus that directly invades neurons in the brainstem and cerebellum, causing the triad of fever, headache, and cerebellar ataxia before the rash even appears.
features: Cerebellar ataxia from direct viral tropism for Purkinje cells, explaining the progressive incoordination and wide-based gait.
Pink macular rash on the thigh reflecting immune complex deposition in small vessels, often appearing after neurological symptoms begin.
Lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose and elevated protein in CSF, consistent with viral neuroinvasion and parenchymal inflammation.
traps: Herpes simplex encephalitis: causes temporal lobe seizures and hemorrhagic necrosis, not cerebellar ataxia; CSF shows red cells and low glucose from necrotizing inflammation.
Cerebellar stroke: abrupt onset with vascular risk factors; CSF is normal and imaging shows ischemic change, not lymphocytic pleocytosis.
Bacterial meningitis: presents with nuchal rigidity, high CSF neutrophils, low glucose, and high protein; no cerebellar signs or rash pattern.
west_nile_encephalitis.clue: Progressive cerebellar ataxia with fever and a macular rash on the thigh, in the setting of normal CSF glucose and elevated lymphocytes.

broad_differential_but_includes_stroke_l.hook: This is a viral encephalitis targeting the cerebellum and brainstem, not a vascular event — the ataxia and fever point to infection, not ischemia.
features: Fever + headache + progressive ataxia: the triad of viral cerebellar inflammation, not stroke (which lacks fever).
Pink macular rash on thigh: a common extraneural sign of West Nile virus, reflecting immune complex deposition.
Elevated CSF lymphocytes with normal glucose: classic viral meningoencephalitis, distinct from bacterial (low glucose) or stroke (normal CSF).
traps: Cerebellar stroke: both cause ataxia, but stroke is acute, afebrile, and lacks rash; CSF is normal.
Bacterial meningitis: presents with fever and headache, but CSF shows low glucose and polymorphonuclear leukocytes, not lymphocytes.
Multiple sclerosis: can cause ataxia and CSF lymphocytosis, but lacks fever and rash, and lesions are typically white matter on MRI.
broad_differential_but_includes_stroke_l.clue: Progressive ataxia with fever and a pink macular rash on the thigh in a 55-year-old woman.
broad_differential_but_includes_stroke_l.diagnosis: Broad differential but includes: Stroke (likely cerebellar stroke)

bacterial_meningitis.hook: The key discriminator here is the normal CSF glucose in viral meningitis versus the low glucose in bacterial meningitis, driven by bacterial consumption of glucose via glycolysis.
features: Low CSF glucose (<40 mg/dL) due to bacterial metabolism and impaired glucose transport across inflamed blood-brain barrier
Elevated CSF protein (>200 mg/dL) from bacterial lysis and inflammatory exudate causing increased permeability
Neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis (typically >1000 cells/µL) reflecting acute bacterial invasion and neutrophil chemotaxis
traps: Viral meningitis: Normal CSF glucose, lymphocytic predominance, lower protein — no bacterial glycolysis or neutrophil recruitment
Fungal meningitis: Low glucose but lymphocytic predominance and slower onset — no acute neutrophil surge
Cerebellar stroke: No CSF pleocytosis or hypoglycorrhachia — purely ischemic mechanism
bacterial_meningitis.clue: CSF glucose <40 mg/dL with >1000 neutrophils/µL and protein >200 mg/dL

viral_meningitis.hook: The core mechanism here is a flavivirus neuroinvasion targeting the cerebellum and brainstem, not just the meninges — the ataxia is the physical clue that this is encephalitis, not simple viral meningitis.
features: Progressive ataxia from direct cerebellar viral invasion — meningitis alone does not cause this.
Macular rash on the thigh — a peripheral viral exanthem from hematogenous spread, not a meningeal sign.
Fever + headache with normal glucose and lymphocytic pleocytosis — the CSF profile of viral meningitis, but the focal neurology (ataxia) points to parenchymal infection.
traps: Viral meningitis — both have headache, fever, and lymphocytic pleocytosis, but encephalitis adds altered mental status or focal signs (here: ataxia) because the virus invades brain parenchyma, not just the subarachnoid space.
Cerebellar stroke — acute ataxia can mimic, but stroke lacks fever, rash, and the prodromal headache; imaging would show ischemia, not the diffuse inflammation of encephalitis.
viral_meningitis.clue: Progressive ataxia in a febrile patient with a macular rash — this combination forces you to think of viral encephalitis (like West Nile) rather than isolated meningitis or stroke.

sepsis.hook: This is not sepsis—the core mechanism is viral neuroinvasion causing direct neuronal injury and cerebellar inflammation, not systemic vasodilation from cytokine storm.
features: Progressive ataxia and cerebellar signs localize to posterior fossa inflammation, not the global hypoperfusion of sepsis.
Macular rash on thigh reflects viral exanthem from hematogenous dissemination to skin, not petechiae from DIC or coagulopathy.
Lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose in CSF indicates viral meningoencephalitis, contrasting with septic meningitis which is neutrophilic with low glucose.
traps: Sepsis: Both have fever, but sepsis causes distributive shock with hypotension and end-organ hypoperfusion, not focal cerebellar findings or a viral rash.
Bacterial meningitis: Both cause headache and fever, but bacterial meningitis presents with neutrophilic CSF, low glucose, and high protein, not lymphocytic predominance with normal glucose.
sepsis.clue: Progressive ataxia with fever and a macular rash on the thigh—this points to viral neurotropism, not bacterial or systemic inflammation.

intracranial_abscess.hook: Intracranial abscess is a focal, encapsulated collection of pus that causes mass effect and localized neurological deficits, whereas West Nile encephalitis is a diffuse viral inflammation of the brain parenchyma causing bilateral, often symmetric symptoms.
features: Focal neurological signs (e.g., unilateral weakness, cranial nerve palsy) due to mass effect of the abscess, not diffuse cortical irritation.
Progressive headache with signs of increased intracranial pressure (papilledema, vomiting) from the expanding lesion, not acute fever and meningeal signs.
Peripheral source of infection (e.g., sinusitis, otitis, dental abscess) seeding the brain via hematogenous spread or contiguous extension.
traps: Viral encephalitis: both present with fever, headache, and altered mental status, but abscess causes focal deficits and papilledema, while encephalitis shows diffuse EEG slowing and CSF lymphocytosis with normal glucose.
Stroke: both cause focal deficits, but abscess has subacute progression over days to weeks, fever, and risk factors for infection, whereas stroke is acute and afebrile.
Brain tumor: both can cause mass effect and headache, but abscess has fever, leukocytosis, and rapid progression over days, while tumor progresses over months without infectious signs.
intracranial_abscess.clue: Look for a peripheral source of infection (e.g., sinusitis, otitis, dental abscess) or a predisposing condition (endocarditis, lung abscess) that seeds the brain; the absence of such a source and presence of diffuse symptoms like ataxia and macular rash favors West Nile encephalitis.

herpes_simplex.hook: Herpes Simplex encephalitis is a hemorrhagic, necrotizing infection of the temporal lobes, while West Nile encephalitis targets the basal ganglia and thalamus with a non-hemorrhagic, lymphocytic CSF.
features: Fever, headache, and progressive ataxia localize to cerebellar involvement, which is classic for West Nile but not HSV.
Pink macular lesions on the thigh suggest a viral exanthem, seen in West Nile but absent in HSV encephalitis.
Normal glucose, elevated lymphocytes, and increased protein in CSF fit viral meningoencephalitis, but HSV often shows red blood cells or xanthochromia due to hemorrhagic necrosis.
traps: Both present with fever and altered mental status, but HSV has acute temporal lobe signs (personality change, aphasia, focal seizures) versus West Nile's cerebellar and basal ganglia symptoms (ataxia, tremor, parkinsonism).
HSV CSF may mimic bacterial infection with low glucose if hemorrhagic, but West Nile maintains normal glucose.
herpes_simplex.clue: Ataxia with a macular rash on the leg points to West Nile, not HSV.

head_trauma.hook: In head trauma, headache and ataxia would arise from direct mechanical disruption or mass effect, not from viral inflammation of the brain parenchyma.
features: Immediate temporal link between blunt force and symptom onset — not days of fever evolving into ataxia.
Focal neurological deficits that correspond to a contusion or hematoma location (e.g., unilateral weakness, cranial nerve palsies) rather than diffuse cerebellar signs.
Absence of systemic prodrome (fever, rash) — the pink macular rash here is a hallmark of West Nile's viral exanthem, not a post-traumatic finding.
traps: Cerebellar stroke — both can cause sudden ataxia, but stroke lacks fever/rash and has a vascular territory pattern on MRI; head trauma would have a clear mechanical history and often scalp signs.

Bacterial meningitis — both cause headache and fever, but bacterial meningitis yields nuchal rigidity and CSF with low glucose/high neutrophils, whereas head trauma would have bloody CSF if subarachnoid hemorrhage is present.
head_trauma.clue: A clear history of a fall or blow to the head just before symptoms began.

multiple_sclerosis.hook: This is a viral encephalitis targeting the brainstem and cerebellum, not a demyelinating white matter attack, which is why the ataxia and fever are simultaneous rather than separated in time.
features: Acute onset of fever and headache preceding neurological deficits — viral prodrome before CNS invasion.
Cerebellar ataxia with macular rash — flavivirus (WNV) often involves cerebellum and can cause a roseolar or maculopapular rash, unlike MS.
