Pseudogout: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals (positively birefringent, rhomboid) cause similar acute inflammation. Differentiate by crystal morphology and birefringence under polarized light.
acute_gout.clue: Look for podagra (first MTP involvement) or a history of hyperuricemia, and confirm with synovial fluid analysis showing urate crystals without organisms.

proximal_tibiofibular_joint_sprain_patel.hook: In disseminated gonococcal infection, the knee is not just painful—it is a hot, tense, chemical synovitis where neutrophils flood the joint space because Neisseria lipooligosaccharide directly activates TLR4 on synovial macrophages, triggering an explosive cytokine cascade that bypasses the usual mechanical wear-and-tear mechanisms of sprains or meniscal tears.
features: Acute monoarticular knee pain with systemic signs (fever, chills, tachycardia) because the bacterial lipooligosaccharide triggers a systemic inflammatory response, unlike the localized, afebrile pain of a sprain or meniscal tear.

Erythema, warmth, and tense effusion on exam due to massive neutrophil infiltration into the synovial space, driven by IL-8 and complement activation—contrast with the cool, non-erythematous effusion of patellofemoral syndrome or meniscal irritation.

Severe pain with any passive range of motion because the inflamed synovium is stretched by the effusion, and the high intra-articular pressure directly stimulates nociceptors—unlike the mechanical click or catch of a meniscal tear or the retropatellar grinding of PFPS.
traps: Gout/pseudogout: Both cause acute monoarthritis with effusion and warmth, but gout is driven by monosodium urate crystals (not bacteria) and typically lacks the migratory tenosynovitis and pustules seen in disseminated gonococcal infection; synovial fluid shows negative birefringent crystals, not gram-negative diplococci.

Lyme disease arthritis: Can cause knee monoarthritis with effusion, but it is typically episodic, less acutely painful, and lacks the high fever, chills, and pustular skin lesions of gonococcemia; synovial fluid WBC is lower and Gram stain is negative.

Acute HIV infection: May present with fever, arthralgias, and rash, but arthritis is usually polyarticular and non-erosive, with a negative Gram stain and no purulent synovial fluid; HIV RNA or p24 antigen would be positive.
proximal_tibiofibular_joint_sprain_patel.clue: The presence of migratory tenosynovitis and pustular skin lesions on exam—these are the hallmark of disseminated gonococcal infection and are never seen in mechanical knee pathology.
proximal_tibiofibular_joint_sprain_patel.diagnosis: Proximal Tibiofibular Joint Sprain, Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome, or Meniscal Tear (common causes of knee pain)

giardiasis.hook: This parasite colonizes the duodenum and proximal jejunum, physically coating the brush border — it doesn't invade, so the mechanism is malabsorption (steatorrhea) from mechanical blockade of fat absorption, not inflammation.
features: Foul-smelling, greasy, floating stools (steatorrhea) from malabsorbed fat — direct result of Giardia trophozoites carpeting the duodenal epithelium and blocking micelle formation
Bloating and sulfurous belching — from bacterial fermentation of undigested carbohydrates and the parasite's own metabolic gas production in the proximal small bowel
Weight loss despite normal appetite — caloric deprivation from malabsorption, not anorexia (unlike invasive pathogens)
traps: Celiac disease — both cause steatorrhea and bloating, but Giardia lacks the anti-tTG antibody and has a travel/camping trigger with rapid onset; also, Giardia responds to metronidazole, not gluten withdrawal
Irritable bowel syndrome — can have bloating and diarrhea, but IBS stool is not greasy/foul-smelling because there's no fat malabsorption; Giardia's stool has visible oil and floats

C. difficile — also causes foul diarrhea after antibiotics, but C. diff is watery/mucoid (colitis), not steatorrheic (small bowel); C. diff has pseudomembranes on colonoscopy, Giardia has normal mucosa
giardiasis.clue: Foul-smelling, greasy, floating stools that are difficult to flush after drinking untreated stream water on a camping trip — this is not just diarrhea, it's steatorrhea from a small bowel parasite.

amebiasis.hook: Amebiasis is a colonic mucosal invasion by Entamoeba histolytica causing bloody diarrhea, whereas Giardia is a small bowel luminal parasite causing malabsorptive steatorrhea.
features: Bloody or mucoid diarrhea due to colonic tissue invasion and lytic necrosis from amebic trophozoites.
Tenesmus and abdominal pain from rectosigmoid inflammation, often with systemic symptoms like fever and weight loss.
Hepatic abscess risk: amebae travel via portal vein to liver, causing right upper quadrant pain and fever without frank diarrhea.
traps: Giardiasis: mechanism is small bowel luminal attachment causing malabsorption and steatorrhea, not colonic invasion, so stool is greasy/foul-smelling, not bloody.
Bacterial dysentery (Shigella, Salmonella): also colonic invasion but causes acute, high-fever dysentery with fecal leukocytes; amebiasis is more subacute with fewer WBCs in stool.
Inflammatory bowel disease: chronic colonic inflammation causes bloody diarrhea, but lacks travel history and has extraintestinal manifestations like arthritis, plus granulomas on biopsy.
amebiasis.clue: Foul-smelling, greasy diarrhea with recent camping trip drinking untreated water points to Giardia, not the bloody mucoid stools of amebiasis.

infectious_diarrhea_including_bacterial.hook: Giardia attaches to duodenal epithelium, physically coating the brush border and blocking fat absorption, causing steatorrhea without invading the mucosa or causing fever.
features: Foul-smelling, greasy, floating stools (steatorrhea) from malabsorption of fats due to mechanical blockade of brush border enzymes by Giardia trophozoites.
Bloating and abdominal cramps from bacterial fermentation of unabsorbed nutrients in the colon.
Weight loss despite normal appetite because calories are lost in stool, not from systemic illness or anorexia.
traps: Bacterial diarrhea (e.g., Campylobacter, Salmonella): Causes fever, bloody stools, and tenesmus from mucosal invasion and inflammation—Giardia lacks these features because it stays in the lumen.
Celiac disease: Also presents with steatorrhea and weight loss but is triggered by gluten, not travel, and has elevated tissue transglutaminase antibodies, not Giardia antigen.
Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS): Can have bloating and diarrhea but stool is not greasy/foul-smelling and there is no weight loss because no malabsorption occurs.
infectious_diarrhea_including_bacterial.clue: History of drinking untreated stream water on a camping trip in a patient with foul-smelling, greasy diarrhea and weight loss without fever.

viral.hook: The mechanism here is that Giardia trophozoites coat the duodenal mucosa, disrupting brush border disaccharidases and physically blocking fat absorption—so the diarrhea is greasy and foul due to unabsorbed fat, not watery or bloody.
features: Steatorrhea (foul, greasy, floats) because Giardia damages microvilli and deconjugates bile salts, preventing micelle formation and fat absorption.
Bloating and cramps from bacterial fermentation of unabsorbed carbohydrates (disaccharidase deficiency).
Weight loss with normal appetite due to malabsorption of macronutrients, not from dehydration or anorexia.
traps: Amebiasis (E. histolytica) causes bloody, mucoid diarrhea (dysentery) because it invades colonic mucosa, not the small bowel—so no steatorrhea or weight loss.
Bacterial enteritis (e.g., Campylobacter, Salmonella) typically presents with acute, watery or bloody diarrhea and fever due to inflammation and toxin-mediated secretion, not chronic greasy stools.
Celiac disease also causes steatorrhea, but it’s triggered by gluten, not by a travel-related protozoan—and small bowel biopsy shows villous atrophy, not adherent trophozoites.
viral.clue: Greasy, foul-smelling diarrhea that floats in a patient with recent untreated water exposure (camping, hiking, travel).

parasitic.hook: Giardia attaches to the duodenal brush border, physically blocking fat absorption and causing steatorrhea, which explains the greasy, foul-smelling diarrhea here.
features: Chronic steatorrhea (greasy, foul-smelling stools) from Giardia's physical coating of the duodenal mucosa, preventing micelle formation and fat digestion.
Bloating and abdominal cramps due to gas production from undigested carbohydrates being fermented by colonic bacteria.
Weight loss from malabsorption of fats and carbohydrates, driven by the parasitic barrier rather than mucosal destruction.
traps: Amebiasis: causes bloody, mucoid diarrhea (dysentery) via invasive trophozoites that lyse colonic epithelium, not steatorrhea.
C. difficile: watery, foul-smelling diarrhea from toxin-mediated colitis, but lacks steatorrhea and travel to untreated water source.
Bacterial enteritis (e.g., Campylobacter): acute inflammatory diarrhea with fever and bloody stools, not chronic greasy stools without fever.
parasitic.clue: History of drinking untreated stream water during a camping trip is the single discriminating trigger for Giardia.

inflammatory_bowel_disease.hook: Giardia disrupts the brush border, causing malabsorptive steatorrhea with bloating and cramps, whereas IBD is a transmural inflammatory process driven by immune dysregulation.
features: Foul-smelling, greasy, floating stools (steatorrhea) from impaired fat absorption due to Giardia's physical coating of the duodenal epithelium.
Bloating and flatulence from bacterial over-fermentation of unabsorbed carbohydrates in the colon.
Weight loss and fatigue from chronic malabsorption of nutrients, not from systemic inflammation.
traps: IBD: Presents with bloody, mucoid diarrhea and tenesmus from colonic ulceration, not steatorrhea; driven by immune-mediated inflammation, not brush border disruption.
Celiac disease: Also causes steatorrhea and bloating, but triggered by gluten-induced autoimmune enteropathy, not a protozoan; serology and biopsy show villous atrophy with lymphocytosis.

Irritable bowel syndrome: Causes bloating and altered stool frequency, but stools are not greasy or foul-smelling, and weight loss is absent; mechanism is visceral hypersensitivity and dysmotility, not malabsorption.
inflammatory_bowel_disease.clue: Recent camping trip with untreated stream water ingestion is the key trigger for Giardia exposure, pointing to an infectious cause over IBD.

food_poisoning.hook: The foul-smelling, greasy, floating stool (steatorrhea) is the signature of Giardia's mechanism: the trophozoite carpeting the duodenal and jejunal mucosa, physically blocking fat absorption.
features: Steatorrhea: greasy, foul-smelling, floating stool occurs because Giardia trophozoites attach to the duodenal/jejunal brush border, creating a physical barrier to micelle formation and fat digestion.
Bloating and foul gas: the undigested carbohydrates in the colon are fermented by bacteria, producing gas; the sulfur-containing compounds from the protozoan's metabolism add the putrid odor.
Weight loss with normal appetite: despite eating, the malabsorption of fat and carbohydrates means calories are lost in stool, not absorbed.
traps: Bacterial gastroenteritis (e.g., Campylobacter, Salmonella): causes acute, watery or bloody diarrhea with fever, not the chronic, insidious steatorrhea and weight loss; bacteria invade mucosa causing inflammation, not just surface blockade.

Celiac disease: also causes steatorrhea and weight loss, but triggered by gluten, not travel to endemic water; serology (tTG IgA) and duodenal biopsy show villous atrophy, not Giardia cysts or trophozoites.
food_poisoning.clue: Recent camping/hiking trip drinking untreated stream water is the classic exposure for Giardia cysts.

hepatitis_a.hook: Hepatitis A causes diarrhea through cholestatic liver injury disrupting bile acid delivery to the gut, unlike Giardia which directly impairs fat absorption by coating the duodenal mucosa.
features: Prodromal nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea followed by jaundice and dark urine (bilirubinuria) from acute hepatocyte necrosis.
Stools are pale/clay-colored due to obstructive pattern from intrahepatic cholestasis, not steatorrhea from malabsorption.
Right upper quadrant tenderness and elevated transaminases (ALT/AST >10x ULN) with positive IgM anti-HAV confirm acute viral hepatitis.
traps: Giardia: causes steatorrhea via trophozoite attachment disrupting brush border enzymes, not biliary obstruction; no jaundice or transaminitis.
Amebiasis: produces bloody mucoid diarrhea from colonic invasion, not pale stools or hepatobiliary enzyme elevation.
C. difficile: diarrhea from toxin-mediated colitis, often with fever and leukocytosis, lacking the cholestatic pattern of hepatitis.
hepatitis_a.clue: Diarrhea followed by jaundice and clay-colored stools in a patient with recent travel to endemic area.

c_difficile_infection.hook: In C. diff, the diarrhea is driven by toxin-mediated colonic inflammation and pseudomembrane formation, not by the small intestinal malabsorption seen in Giardia.
features: Watery, non-bloody diarrhea with a distinct foul odor, often with mucus, driven by C. diff toxins A and B causing colonic epithelial necrosis and neutrophil recruitment.
Diarrhea typically follows antibiotic use (e.g., clindamycin, fluoroquinolones) within weeks, as disruption of colonic microbiota allows C. diff overgrowth.
Systemic signs like fever, leukocytosis, and abdominal tenderness reflect toxin-induced colitis, unlike the malabsorptive, steatorrheal pattern of Giardia.
traps: Giardiasis: Both cause foul-smelling diarrhea, but Giardia is small-intestinal → steatorrhea (greasy, floating stools) and bloating from malabsorption, while C. diff is colonic → watery, inflammatory diarrhea with WBCs.
IBD flare: Can mimic C. diff with bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain, but C. diff is infectious (toxin assay positive) and typically linked to antibiotic exposure.

Other infectious colitis (e.g., Shigella, Salmonella): Also cause inflammatory diarrhea, but C. diff has a unique toxin-mediated pathogenesis and is not associated with travel or contaminated water (unlike Giardia).
c_difficile_infection.clue: Antibiotic use within the past 8 weeks is the single most specific trigger for C. diff infection, distinguishing it from travel-related parasitic causes.

irritable_bowel_syndrome.hook: Giardia causes malabsorptive diarrhea by coating the duodenal brush border, not by osmotic or secretory mechanisms like IBS or bacterial toxins.
features: Foul-smelling, greasy stools (steatorrhea) from fat malabsorption due to brush border damage.
Symptoms triggered by untreated water exposure, not by stress or diet as in IBS.
Weight loss and bloating from nutrient malabsorption, not from altered motility alone.
traps: IBS-D: Pain improves with defecation, stools are watery/mucous but not greasy, and weight loss is absent; mechanism is visceral hypersensitivity and altered motility, not mucosal damage.
Celiac disease: Also causes steatorrhea but is triggered by gluten, not water exposure, and has serologic markers (anti-tTG).
Bacterial gastroenteritis: Acute, watery diarrhea from enterotoxin or invasion, but stools are not persistently greasy; fever and fecal leukocytes are common.
irritable_bowel_syndrome.clue: Recent camping trip with untreated stream water and foul-smelling, greasy diarrhea.

celiac_disease.hook: In celiac disease, the diarrhea is driven by an autoimmune attack on the small intestinal villi triggered by gluten, leading to malabsorption of fat and nutrients — whereas in giardiasis, the mechanism is a parasitic infection that coats the duodenal epithelium, causing direct interference with fat absorption and a similar steatorrhea.
features: Chronic, foul-smelling, greasy diarrhea (steatorrhea) from fat malabsorption due to villous atrophy and loss of brush-border enzymes.
Bloating and abdominal cramps from bacterial fermentation of unabsorbed nutrients in the colon.
Weight loss and nutritional deficiencies (iron, folate, vitamin D) due to impaired absorption in the damaged proximal small intestine.
traps: Giardiasis: Both cause steatorrhea and bloating, but giardia is an acute infection after drinking contaminated water, and the diarrhea is often more explosive and watery with nausea; celiac is chronic, triggered by gluten, and associated with extra-intestinal signs like dermatitis herpetiformis or iron-deficiency anemia.

Tropical sprue: Also causes chronic steatorrhea after travel to endemic areas, but it is due to bacterial overgrowth and responds to antibiotics, not gluten withdrawal; celiac has specific serologic markers (tTG IgA) and HLA-DQ2/DQ8 association.

Irritable bowel syndrome: Can present with bloating and diarrhea, but stool is typically not greasy or foul-smelling, and there is no malabsorption or weight loss — the mechanism is altered gut motility and visceral hypersensitivity, not structural damage.
celiac_disease.clue: Diarrhea that worsens with gluten ingestion and improves with gluten avoidance, plus positive tissue transglutaminase IgA antibodies.

crohn_s_disease.hook: Crohn’s is a transmural granulomatous inflammation that can mimic Giardia’s steatorrhea, but its mechanism is immune-driven stricturing and fistulization, not luminal trophozoite attachment.
features: Steatorrhea from terminal ileal inflammation impairing bile acid reabsorption and fat absorption—not from trophozoite coating of the brush border as in Giardia.
Abdominal pain often right lower quadrant with palpable mass or fullness from transmural inflammation and creeping fat, not epigastric cramps from duodenal/jejunal parasite burden.
Weight loss driven by chronic cytokine-mediated anorexia and malabsorption, not acute caloric loss from diarrhea alone.
traps: Giardiasis: both cause steatorrhea and bloating, but Giardia’s mechanism is mechanical barrier disruption by trophozoites coating the duodenal epithelium, not transmural inflammation; Crohn’s has skip lesions, fistulas, and perianal disease.
Irritable bowel syndrome: IBS-D has urgency and bloating but no malabsorption or weight loss—pathophysiology is visceral hypersensitivity and dysmotility, not structural inflammation.

Celiac disease: also causes steatorrhea and weight loss but is gluten-triggered intraepithelial lymphocytosis and villous atrophy in the proximal small bowel, not transmural or ileal-predominant inflammation.
crohn_s_disease.clue: History of perianal abscess or fistula, or right lower quadrant mass on exam, points to Crohn’s over Giardia.

gastroenteritis.hook: Giardia attaches to duodenal epithelium, coating it like a biofilm that physically blocks fat absorption, causing steatorrhea and gas from undigested fats hitting colonic bacteria.
features: Foul-smelling, greasy diarrhea (steatorrhea) because the organism's ventral disk mechanically obstructs micelle formation and fat digestion.
Bloating and sulfurous belching from bacterial fermentation of malabsorbed fats and carbohydrates in the colon.
Weight loss despite normal appetite due to calorie loss from fat malabsorption.
traps: Celiac disease: Both cause steatorrhea and bloating, but Giardia has acute onset after water exposure and responds to antiparasitics, not gluten withdrawal.
Tropical sprue: Also causes malabsorption post-travel, but Giardia has specific stool antigen/microscopy findings and responds to metronidazole.
Irritable bowel syndrome: Bloating and cramps overlap, but IBS does not cause steatorrhea or weight loss.
gastroenteritis.clue: Foul-smelling, greasy, floating stools with recent untreated stream water ingestion.

opioid_overdose.hook: This patient's unresponsiveness is driven by opioid agonism at mu receptors in the brainstem, which suppresses the medullary respiratory center and the pupilloconstrictor nucleus, explaining the respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils.
features: Pinpoint pupils (miosis) from parasympathetic activation at the Edinger-Westphal nucleus, which is uniquely spared in other sedative overdoses.
Respiratory depression (RR <12) due to direct inhibition of the pre-Bötzinger complex, the brainstem's respiratory pacemaker — sedatives like benzodiazepines depress respiration less potently.
Decreased bowel sounds from opioid-induced inhibition of the myenteric plexus, slowing peristalsis — a finding not seen in TCA or salicylate overdose.
traps: TCA overdose: causes anticholinergic symptoms (dilated pupils, tachycardia, hyperthermia) and seizures — the opposite pupillary and autonomic picture.
Benzodiazepine overdose: causes sedation and respiratory depression but pupils are normal or minimally reactive, not pinpoint, and bowel sounds are preserved.
opioid_overdose.clue: Bilateral pinpoint pupils that do not dilate with naloxone administration suggests an alternative cause like pontine hemorrhage, but if they reverse with naloxone, it's pathognomonic for opioid overdose.

narcotic_overdose.hook: Opioid overdose is a toxidrome of μ-receptor agonism causing brainstem depression — pinpoint pupils from Edinger-Westphal nucleus activation, and bradypnea from medullary respiratory center suppression.
features: Pinpoint (miotic) pupils due to parasympathetic activation at the Edinger-Westphal nucleus — unopposed sphincter pupillae tone.
Respiratory rate <12 (often <8) from direct depression of medullary pre-Bötzinger complex and chemoreceptors.
Decreased bowel sounds from inhibition of myenteric plexus acetylcholine release — opioid-induced ileus.
traps: Pontine hemorrhage (e.g., basilar artery thrombosis) can also cause pinpoint pupils with coma, but respiratory pattern is Cheyne-Stokes or ataxic, not depressed; and no bowel sound changes.
Clonidine overdose mimics miosis and bradypnea but also causes hypotension and bradycardia via central α2 agonism — lacks ileus and responds to naloxone partially or not at all.
Organophosphate poisoning causes miosis and bradypnea but with hypersalivation, lacrimation, fasciculations, and diarrhea — cholinergic excess, not opioid.
narcotic_overdose.clue: Unresponsive patient with miosis and respiratory rate <12 — give naloxone immediately.

tca_overdose.hook: TCA overdose causes unresponsiveness through sodium channel blockade leading to widened QRS and hypotension, not through opioid receptor agonism causing miosis and bradypnea.
features: Widened QRS >100ms from sodium channel blockade, often with R wave in aVR >3mm, leading to ventricular dysrhythmias and seizures.
Anticholinergic signs (dilated pupils, flushed skin, dry mucosa, urinary retention) from muscarinic receptor blockade.
Hypotension from alpha-1 blockade and myocardial depression, not from respiratory depression alone.
traps: Opioid overdose: Both cause unresponsiveness, but opioid has pinpoint pupils (miosis) from mu-receptor agonism, while TCA has dilated pupils from anticholinergic effect.
Seizures: TCA-induced seizures result from sodium channel blockade and GABA antagonism, not from hypoxia as in opioid overdose.
Hypotension: In TCA, it's due to alpha blockade and direct myocardial depression; in opioid, it's secondary to respiratory depression and hypoxia.
tca_overdose.clue: Wide-complex tachycardia on ECG with anticholinergic signs (dilated pupils, flushed skin) in an unresponsive patient.

aspirin_overdose.hook: Aspirin overdose drives a pure metabolic acidosis with a compensatory respiratory alkalosis from direct brainstem stimulation, not respiratory depression.
features: Tinnitus and hyperventilation due to salicylate-induced central respiratory drive and cochlear toxicity — not the bradypnea of opioids.
Mixed acid-base disorder: primary respiratory alkalosis plus high anion gap metabolic acidosis from uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation.
Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema in severe cases from increased capillary permeability — not from opioid-induced hypoventilation.
traps: Opioid overdose: both can cause unresponsiveness, but opioids produce miosis and bradypnea (respiratory depression), while aspirin causes tinnitus and tachypnea (respiratory stimulation) with a normal or wide pupils.
Diabetic ketoacidosis: both cause high anion gap metabolic acidosis and Kussmaul breathing, but aspirin also induces respiratory alkalosis and tinnitus, without hyperglycemia or ketonemia.
Sepsis: both can cause tachypnea and altered mental status, but aspirin lacks fever, hypotension, or leukocytosis, and the acid-base pattern is distinctive.
aspirin_overdose.clue: Tinnitus plus tachypnea with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis and a normal or elevated pH (mixed respiratory alkalosis) — impossible in pure opioid overdose.

toxic_alcohol_ingestion.hook: Toxic alcohol ingestion causes a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with an elevated osmolar gap, not the opioid toxidrome of miosis and respiratory depression.
features: Elevated osmolar gap (measured osmolality - calculated osmolality > 10) due to the alcohol itself early on.
High anion gap metabolic acidosis from toxic metabolites (e.g., formic acid from methanol, oxalic acid from ethylene glycol).

End-organ effects specific to alcohol type: visual disturbances (methanol), oxalate crystals in urine and acute kidney injury (ethylene glycol), or profound hypoglycemia and ketosis (isopropyl alcohol).
traps: Ethanol intoxication also causes unresponsiveness and respiratory depression, but it typically causes an elevated osmolar gap without a high anion gap metabolic acidosis (unless alcoholic ketoacidosis supervenes).

Diabetic ketoacidosis can present with high anion gap acidosis and altered mental status, but lacks an elevated osmolar gap and the specific end-organ findings (e.g., oxalate crystals, visual changes).
toxic_alcohol_ingestion.clue: The presence of an elevated osmolar gap on initial labs before the acidosis fully develops.

ethanol_poisoning.hook: Ethanol poisoning causes unresponsiveness via global CNS depression through GABA agonism and NMDA antagonism, without the pinpoint pupils or respiratory depression of opioid overdose.
features: Ethanol leads to dose-dependent CNS depression, but at toxic levels, nystagmus, ataxia, and slurred speech precede stupor—unlike opioids where miosis and bradypnea dominate.
Hypoglycemia is a key feature in ethanol poisoning due to impaired gluconeogenesis, which is not a mechanism in opioid overdose.
Osmolal gap elevation is specific to ethanol (and other toxic alcohols) from increased serum osmolality, not seen in opioid intoxication.
traps: Opioid overdose: Both cause CNS depression, but opioids cause miosis and respiratory depression via mu-receptor agonism, while ethanol does not cause pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression is less prominent.

Other toxic alcohols (methanol, ethylene glycol): They also cause osmolal gap and CNS depression, but ethanol typically lacks the metabolic acidosis and retinal toxicity of methanol or the oxalate crystals and renal failure of ethylene glycol.
ethanol_poisoning.clue: Check for hypoglycemia and osmolal gap—if present with unresponsiveness but no miosis, suspect ethanol over opioids.

acetaminophen_overdose.hook: Acetaminophen overdose lacks the anticholinergic and opioid features of the case's toxidrome; its mechanism is direct hepatocyte necrosis via NAPQI, not CNS depression.
features: Silent initial 24 hours: no miosis, no respiratory depression, no altered mental status until fulminant hepatic failure sets in (days later).
Nausea/vomiting may occur early but are non-specific and driven by GI mucosal irritation, not CNS mechanisms.
Laboratory clue: elevated transaminases (AST>ALT) with a delayed INR rise, contrasting with the immediate pinpoint pupils and bradypnea of opioids.
traps: Opioid overdose: both can present with unresponsiveness, but acetaminophen overdose does not cause miosis or respiratory depression; instead, it causes a delayed hepatotoxicity.
TCA overdose: both may cause coma, but TCA overdose produces anticholinergic signs (dilated pupils, tachycardia, QRS widening) and seizures, not the silent hepatic necrosis of acetaminophen.
acetaminophen_overdose.clue: No miosis, no respiratory depression, and normal initial mental status unless co-ingested; transaminitis days later is the hallmark.

other_medication_overdose.hook: This is opioid overdose: the opioid receptor agonism in the brainstem drives the triad of miosis, respiratory depression, and CNS depression — each tied to specific receptor populations (mu-2 for respiration, mu-1 for miosis).
features: Pinpoint pupils (miosis) from parasympathetic activation via Edinger-Westphal nucleus mu-receptor agonism — this is opioid-specific and not seen in sedative-hypnotic or ethanol overdose.
Respiratory depression (rate < 12) due to decreased medullary chemoreceptor sensitivity to CO2 — this is the lethal mechanism, directly reversed by naloxone.
Decreased bowel sounds from mu-receptor inhibition of peristalsis in the enteric nervous system — a peripheral clue that reinforces the central toxidrome.
traps: Sedative-hypnotic overdose (e.g., benzodiazepines, barbiturates): causes CNS/respiratory depression but pupils are normal or dilated — no miosis because GABAergic drugs don't activate the Edinger-Westphal nucleus.
Ethanol overdose: respiratory depression and coma are possible, but pupils are reactive and often dilated — ethanol potentiates GABA but does not stimulate the pupilloconstrictor pathway.
Clonidine overdose: can cause miosis, bradycardia, and hypotension, but respiratory rate is typically preserved — clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist, not a mu-agonist, so naloxone won't reverse it.
other_medication_overdose.clue: Pinpoint pupils (1-2 mm) in a patient with respiratory depression and unresponsiveness — this is the single most discriminating physical exam finding for opioid overdose over other sedative ingestions.

benzodiazepine_overdose_diazepam.hook: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A tone to cause sedation without the pinpoint pupils or respiratory depression out of proportion to sedation that defines opioid toxidrome.
features: Sedation with normal or near-normal pupillary size (no miosis) because GABA agonism does not alter pupillary sympathetic or parasympathetic balance.

Respiratory depression only at high doses and typically less severe than opioids for equivalent sedation depth, since benzos depress central respiratory drive indirectly via GABA potentiation rather than direct mu-receptor agonism on brainstem respiratory centers.
Preserved bowel sounds or mild ileus only at very high doses, because GABA modulation does not directly inhibit enteric nervous system motility like mu-opioid receptor activation does.
traps: Opioid overdose: Both cause unresponsiveness and respiratory depression, but opioids produce pathognomonic pinpoint pupils (miosis) from Edinger-West nucleus stimulation, whereas benzos do not change pupillary size.
TCA overdose: Both can cause sedation, but TCAs additionally cause anticholinergic signs (dilated pupils, tachycardia, dry skin) and QRS widening on EKG, absent in pure benzodiazepine overdose.
Ethanol intoxication: Both are GABAergic sedatives, but ethanol also causes nystagmus, hypoglycemia, and often a smell of alcohol on breath, while benzodiazepine overdose lacks these features.
benzodiazepine_overdose_diazepam.clue: Unresponsive patient with normal pupils and no opioid stigmata (needle marks, miosis, constipation) but with a history of prescribed benzodiazepines or empty pill bottles.

guillain_barre_syndrome.hook: The immune system, tricked by molecular mimicry from a recent infection, launches an antibody attack against peripheral nerve myelin, producing rapid, symmetric, ascending weakness with areflexia.
features: Rapidly progressive, symmetric ascending weakness starting in the legs – reflects demyelination of peripheral motor nerves in a distal-to-proximal pattern.
Areflexia or hyporeflexia early in the course – due to loss of myelin insulation disrupting saltatory conduction and reflex arc propagation.

Mild sensory symptoms (paresthesias) without prominent objective sensory loss – because large-fiber proprioception is hit but small-fiber pain/temperature are relatively spared; the immune attack targets myelin, not axons.
traps: Myasthenia gravis: weakness is fatigable, not symmetric ascending, and reflexes are preserved; mechanism is postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor blockade, not demyelination.
Acute myelopathy: weakness is often spastic (UMN signs) with a sensory level and hyperreflexia, not areflexic; lesion is in spinal cord, not peripheral nerves.
Conversion disorder: weakness is inconsistent, non-anatomic, and lacks areflexia; no underlying immune-mediated mechanism or antecedent infection.
guillain_barre_syndrome.clue: History of diarrheal illness or respiratory infection 1–3 weeks prior to onset of symmetric ascending weakness with areflexia.

myasthenia_gravis.hook: In myasthenia gravis, the weakness is due to impaired neuromuscular transmission from autoantibodies blocking or destroying postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, not from demyelination of peripheral nerves.
features: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness that worsens with activity and improves with rest, often affecting ocular, bulbar, and proximal limb muscles.
Ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, or dysarthria are common early signs due to cranial nerve involvement.
Deep tendon reflexes are typically normal or brisk, not absent as in Guillain-Barre.
traps: Guillain-Barre Syndrome: Both cause progressive weakness, but GBS is demyelinating (ascending, areflexic, often with paresthesias and antecedent infection) and does not fluctuate with activity.
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome: Also fatigable weakness but improves with sustained contraction, and is associated with small cell lung cancer and autonomic symptoms.
Conversion disorder: Weakness is inconsistent, non-anatomic, and lacks objective findings like ptosis or decremental response on EMG.
myasthenia_gravis.clue: Ask if the weakness fluctuates with activity or time of day, and specifically check for ptosis or diplopia after sustained upgaze.

paraneoplastic_neuropathy.hook: Paraneoplastic neuropathy is a non-metastatic, immune-mediated attack on peripheral nerves driven by onconeural antibodies cross-reacting with tumor antigens, not post-infectious molecular mimicry.
features: Subacute, often asymmetric or multifocal sensorimotor deficits that can precede cancer diagnosis by months.
Prominent neuropathic pain and autonomic dysfunction (e.g., orthostasis, arrhythmias) due to dorsal root ganglion and small-fiber involvement.
Electrophysiology showing axonal loss or mixed demyelination/axonal patterns, often with elevated CSF protein but without the albuminocytologic dissociation of GBS.
traps: Guillain-Barre Syndrome: GBS is acute, symmetric, ascending, triggered by infection (C. jejuni), and primarily demyelinating; paraneoplastic is subacute, often asymmetric, and axonal with onconeural antibodies (e.g., anti-Hu, anti-CV2).

Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP): CIDP has a relapsing-remitting or progressive course with demyelinating features and response to immunotherapy, whereas paraneoplastic neuropathy is relentlessly progressive, associated with malignancy, and often refractory to standard immune modulation.
paraneoplastic_neuropathy.clue: Look for concurrent unexplained weight loss, smoking history, or a known malignancy; the presence of anti-Hu or anti-CV2 antibodies is pathognomonic for paraneoplastic neuropathy over GBS.

hiv_peripheral_neuropathy.hook: HIV peripheral neuropathy is a length-dependent, dying-back axonopathy from viral or drug toxicity, not an immune-mediated demyelination targeting proximal roots.
features: Stocking-glove sensory loss and distal weakness beginning in feet, not ascending proximal spread
Hyporeflexia limited to ankles, not areflexia across all deep tendon reflexes
Painful burning or tingling paresthesias in a symmetric distal gradient
traps: Guillain-Barre Syndrome: immune attack on myelin causes rapid, ascending weakness with diffuse areflexia and frequent respiratory involvement; HIV neuropathy is slower, distal, and spares proximal strength until advanced.
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy: relapsing-remitting or progressive proximal and distal weakness with demyelinating features on NCS/EMG; HIV neuropathy is axonal, not demyelinating.
hiv_peripheral_neuropathy.clue: Presence of distal burning pain and sensory loss in a stocking-glove distribution without respiratory involvement or antecedent diarrheal illness.

conversion_disorder.hook: This is not conversion disorder because the weakness is rooted in molecular mimicry and demyelination, not in psychological dissociation from neurological function.
features: Progressive symmetric ascending weakness with areflexia — this follows a predictable anatomic sequence (distal to proximal) due to immune attack on peripheral myelin, not the non-anatomic, inconsistent pattern of conversion.

Antecedent diarrheal illness (Campylobacter jejuni) triggers molecular mimicry — antibodies cross-react with myelin proteins, causing demyelination; conversion disorder has no such biological trigger.

Respiratory difficulty despite stable vitals — early respiratory muscle involvement is a red flag for demyelinating polyneuropathy, not a conversion symptom, which typically involves voluntary muscle groups without autonomic compromise.
traps: Myasthenia gravis: also presents with weakness, but is fatigable (worsens with use, improves with rest) due to NMJ blockade, not ascending and areflexic like GBS.

Acute myelopathy: presents with weakness and areflexia acutely (spinal shock), but has a sensory level and often sphincter involvement; GBS lacks a discrete sensory level and has more distal paresthesias.
conversion_disorder.clue: Ask about recent diarrheal illness and check for areflexia — if both present, GBS is the mechanism, not conversion.

chronic_inflammatory_demyelinating_polyn.hook: Guillain-Barre is an acute, monophasic, post-infectious demyelination; CIDP is its chronic, progressive or relapsing cousin driven by ongoing T-cell-mediated attack on Schwann cells.
features: Rapidly progressive symmetric ascending weakness with areflexia over days to weeks – the acute tempo reflects widespread simultaneous demyelination triggered by molecular mimicry.

Antecedent diarrheal or respiratory illness (e.g., Campylobacter jejuni) – the immune system mistakes peripheral nerve myelin for bacterial antigens, initiating a self-limited but severe wave of demyelination.

Paresthesias and possible respiratory muscle involvement – demyelination spares axons initially, so sensory symptoms and motor conduction block are widespread, but axonal loss is minimal unless severe.
traps: CIDP – progresses over >8 weeks or relapses, because ongoing T-cell activation causes chronic inflammation and remyelination attempts, not a single antibody-mediated wave.
Myasthenia gravis – fatigable weakness without sensory loss or areflexia, because the defect is at the neuromuscular junction (acetylcholine receptor antibodies), not in peripheral nerve conduction.
Acute myelopathy – spastic paralysis with hyperreflexia and a sensory level, because the lesion is in the central nervous system (spinal cord), not in peripheral nerves.
chronic_inflammatory_demyelinating_polyn.clue: Rapidly progressive symmetric ascending weakness with areflexia and a clear antecedent infection – the combination of tempo, reflex loss, and trigger points to acute immune demyelination.

acute_myelopathy_from.hook: Acute myelopathy causes focal cord-level motor/sensory deficits with hyperreflexia, not the ascending areflexic paralysis of Guillain-Barre.
features: Symmetric ascending weakness with areflexia from antibody-mediated demyelination of peripheral nerves
Autonomic instability (labile BP, arrhythmias) due to involvement of unmyelinated sympathetic fibers
Respiratory muscle weakness from phrenic nerve demyelination, not from high cervical cord lesion
traps: Transverse myelitis: both can cause leg weakness and sensory loss, but myelopathy shows a spinal cord level (e.g., T10 pinprick loss) and hyperreflexia below the lesion, whereas GBS has areflexia and no cord level
Myasthenia gravis: both can cause fluctuating weakness and respiratory compromise, but MG has ptosis/diplopia, fatiguability, and preserved reflexes; GBS has ascending pattern and absent reflexes
acute_myelopathy_from.clue: Areflexia with symmetric ascending weakness and a history of recent diarrheal illness.

acute_coronary_syndrome_acs.hook: Plaque rupture triggers platelet aggregation and thrombus formation, obstructing coronary flow and causing myocardial ischemia—this is why the pain is anginal, not pleuritic or positional.
features: Retrosternal pressure or squeezing lasting >20 minutes, often radiating to left arm, jaw, or back—due to ischemic activation of visceral afferent cardiac nerves (C8–T4).
Pain is constant, not sharp or stabbing, and unrelieved by rest or nitroglycerin in STEMI—because transmural infarction creates irreversible myocyte death with sustained nociceptive signaling.
Associated dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, or syncope—reflecting vagal activation and reduced cardiac output from ischemic pump failure.
traps: Pericarditis: pain is sharp, pleuritic, positional (worse supine, better leaning forward), and often has a pericardial rub—unlike ACS, the mechanism is inflammation of the pericardium, not ischemic myocyte necrosis.
Pulmonary embolism: pain is pleuritic, with sudden dyspnea, hypoxia, and often hemoptysis—mechanism is right ventricular strain from acute pulmonary hypertension, not coronary obstruction.
Costochondritis: pain is reproducible on palpation of the costochondral junctions—this is a musculoskeletal, not ischemic, mechanism.
acute_coronary_syndrome_acs.clue: Ask: 'Is the pain brought on by exertion or emotional stress, and does it go away with rest?'—a positive response strongly favors ischemic mechanism.

tension_pneumothorax.hook: Tension pneumothorax causes chest pain because air trapped in the pleural space under positive pressure compresses the heart and great vessels, reducing venous return and cardiac output—not because of coronary ischemia.
features: Tracheal deviation away from the affected side due to mediastinal shift from positive intrapleural pressure
Distended neck veins from impaired venous return to the right heart
Hypotension and tachycardia from decreased preload and compensatory adrenergic response
traps: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS): pain is ischemic from coronary occlusion, not from pleural pressure; no tracheal deviation or hyperresonance; ECG shows ST changes, not electrical alternans
Cardiac tamponade: also causes hypotension and distended neck veins, but with muffled heart sounds and equalization of diastolic pressures, not hyperresonance or tracheal deviation
Pulmonary embolism: causes pleuritic pain and hypotension but with hypoxia and right heart strain on ECG, not tracheal deviation or unilateral hyperresonance
tension_pneumothorax.clue: Unilateral absent breath sounds with hyperresonance to percussion and tracheal deviation away from that side in a patient with acute dyspnea and chest pain

acute_pericarditis_idiopathic.hook: This chest pain is pleuritic and positional because the inflamed pericardial layers are mechanically rubbing against each other with each breath and change in posture.
features: Sharp, pleuritic chest pain that worsens with inspiration and supine position, and improves with sitting forward — due to direct mechanical irritation of the parietal pericardium against the heart.
Diffuse ST-segment elevation with upward concavity on ECG, reflecting subepicardial myocardial inflammation rather than transmural ischemia.
Pericardial friction rub on auscultation, caused by the inflamed, roughened pericardial surfaces sliding against each other during cardiac motion.
traps: ACS: Pain is typically pressure-like, not pleuritic or positional; ECG shows localized ST elevation with reciprocal depression, not diffuse concave elevation; troponin rises significantly, whereas in pericarditis it is often normal or mildly elevated due to epicardial irritation.
Pleurisy: Pain is also pleuritic but lacks the positional component (worse supine, better leaning forward) and cardiac friction rub; ECG is normal.
acute_pericarditis_idiopathic.clue: Pain that is worse when lying flat and better when leaning forward — a classic mechanical clue that points to pericardial involvement.

panic_attack_panic_disorder.hook: Your chest pain comes from a surge of autonomic output, not from blocked vessels—the mechanism is catecholamine-driven hyperreactivity, not plaque rupture.
features: Chest pain is sharp, fleeting, or pressure-like but shifts with position or breathing, reflecting intercostal muscle tension and hyperventilation-induced esophageal spasm, not fixed ischemic territory.
Palpitations, diaphoresis, and sense of doom coincide with pain onset, driven by a sudden sympathetic storm (norepinephrine surge) rather than gradual ischemic cascade.
Pain peaks within minutes and resolves without troponin elevation, because the trigger is neural (amygdala → locus coeruleus) not vascular (plaque erosion/thrombosis).
traps: ACS: ischemic pain is dull, substernal, radiates to jaw/arm, and is effort-related—caused by fixed stenosis or thrombus, not reversible autonomic spikes.
Costochondritis: reproducible on palpation due to local inflammation, not driven by panic's central autonomic activation.
panic_attack_panic_disorder.clue: Ask: 'Did the chest pain start at rest or during stress/panic?'—if at rest with palpitations and fear, it's panic; if during exertion with radiation, it's ACS.

unstable_angina.hook: Unstable angina is acute myocardial ischemia without necrosis, driven by a dynamic, non-occlusive thrombus over a ruptured plaque that transiently reduces coronary flow.
features: Crescendo pattern: angina that is new, occurs at rest, or is more frequent/severe with minimal exertion, reflecting episodic thrombus formation and lysis.
Pain lasts >20 minutes but resolves without biomarker elevation, because ischemia is severe enough to cause symptoms but not sustained infarction.
ST depression or T-wave inversion on ECG during pain, due to subendocardial ischemia from reduced diastolic perfusion time and increased oxygen demand.
traps: NSTEMI: both present with ST/T changes and rest pain, but NSTEMI has elevated troponin due to irreversible myocyte necrosis from prolonged occlusion.
Stable angina: pain is predictable with exertion and relieved by rest/nitroglycerin, because fixed stenosis causes demand ischemia without plaque rupture or thrombosis.
Prinzmetal angina: also causes rest pain with transient ST elevation, but mechanism is coronary vasospasm (not thrombus) and responds to calcium channel blockers.
unstable_angina.clue: Angina at rest that lasts >20 minutes with normal cardiac biomarkers.

aortic_dissection_stanford_type_a.hook: Aortic dissection tears the intima, allowing blood to track into the media under systemic pressure, creating a false lumen that can propagate, compress true lumen, and cause malperfusion—distinct from the plaque rupture of ACS.
features: Sudden, severe, 'ripping' or 'tearing' chest pain that can migrate to the back or abdomen as the dissection propagates distally.
Pulse or blood pressure differential between limbs due to compression of the true lumen by the false lumen in the aorta.
Widened mediastinum on chest X-ray or intimal flap on CT angiography, confirming the false lumen.
traps: ACS: pain is often crescendo, pressure-like, and radiates to the jaw or left arm; dissection pain is abrupt and migrates with the false lumen.
Pericarditis: pain is pleuritic and positional, without pulse deficits or mediastinal widening.
Pulmonary embolism: pain is pleuritic with dyspnea and right heart strain, not associated with pulse differentials.
aortic_dissection_stanford_type_a.clue: Pain that is maximal at onset and migrates to the back or abdomen, especially with a pulse deficit or blood pressure discrepancy between arms.

atrial_fibrillation.hook: When the atria fibrillate, they lose coordinated contraction, leading to blood stasis in the left atrial appendage that can embolize to coronary arteries, causing chest pain from microvascular obstruction rather than plaque rupture.
features: Irregularly irregular pulse with no discernible P waves on ECG, reflecting chaotic atrial electrical activity that prevents effective mechanical contraction.

Chest pain that is often non-exertional and accompanied by palpitations, dyspnea, or hemodynamic instability, resulting from embolic occlusion of small coronary vessels rather than epicardial stenosis.
Elevated troponin may occur from demand-supply mismatch due to rapid ventricular rate and impaired diastolic filling, not from acute plaque rupture.
traps: ACS from plaque rupture: Here chest pain is typically exertional with ST-segment changes due to fixed epicardial obstruction, whereas AF-related chest pain stems from emboli or rate-related ischemia without ST elevation.
Atrial flutter: Has a sawtooth pattern on ECG with regular R-R intervals, while AF is irregularly irregular due to multiple wandering wavelets, not a single reentrant circuit.
atrial_fibrillation.clue: Absence of ST-segment elevation and presence of an irregularly irregular pulse with no P waves on ECG.

acute_coronary_syndrome_acs_or_other_car.hook: Chest pain from ACS is driven by an abrupt mismatch between myocardial oxygen demand and supply due to plaque rupture and thrombosis, not by inflammation or mechanical stretch.
features: Retrosternal pressure or squeezing that radiates to the left arm, jaw, or shoulder—this is visceral pain from ischemic myocardium, not somatic chest wall pain.
Exertional onset or worsening, relieved by rest or nitroglycerin—oxygen supply-demand mismatch is dynamic, unlike fixed structural pain.
Associated diaphoresis, dyspnea, or nausea—autonomic activation from ischemic myocardium, not from pulmonary or musculoskeletal causes.
traps: Pericarditis: sharp, pleuritic pain that worsens with lying flat and improves leaning forward—mechanism is inflammation of pericardium, not ischemia.
Pulmonary embolism: pleuritic pain with dyspnea, but mechanism is right heart strain from pulmonary vascular occlusion, not myocardial oxygen imbalance.
Costochondritis: localized, reproducible tenderness on palpation—somatic pain from cartilage inflammation, not visceral ischemia.
acute_coronary_syndrome_acs_or_other_car.clue: Ask if the pain is provoked by exertion or emotional stress and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin—this directly tests the supply-demand mismatch mechanism.
acute_coronary_syndrome_acs_or_other_car.diagnosis: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) or other cardiac conditions are the most likely diagnoses for a patient presenting with unknown chest pain

inferior_myocardial_infarction_stemi.hook: Inferior STEMI results from acute occlusion of the right coronary artery (RCA), which supplies the inferior wall via the posterior descending artery, leading to transmural ischemia and injury that produces ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF.
features: ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in leads I and aVL, reflecting transmural ischemia in the inferior wall.
Potential involvement of the right ventricle (RV) if the RCA is occluded proximal to the RV branch, causing ST elevation in right-sided leads (V4R).
High risk of bradyarrhythmias (e.g., sinus bradycardia, AV block) due to RCA supply to the SA and AV nodes, as well as Bezold-Jarisch reflex-mediated vagal activation.
traps: Pericarditis: Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression, no reciprocal changes, and often concave ST segments; mechanism is epicardial inflammation, not transmural ischemia.
Early repolarization: Benign ST elevation with notched J-point and no reciprocal ST depression; due to early repolarization of ventricular myocardium, not ischemia.
Left ventricular aneurysm: Persistent ST elevation after MI without dynamic changes or reciprocal depression; due to mechanical dyskinesis, not acute occlusion.
inferior_myocardial_infarction_stemi.clue: ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in lead aVL.

right_ventricular_myocardial_infarction.hook: The right ventricle is a low-pressure volume pump, so when it infarcts, it can't fill the left ventricle—causing hypotension without pulmonary congestion.
features: Hypotension and jugular venous distention with clear lungs (Kussmaul's sign) because the RV fails to generate enough pressure to overcome systemic venous return.
ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF with reciprocal changes in V1-V2 and ST elevation in V4R (right-sided ECG) due to RCA occlusion proximal to RV branches.
Nitrate-induced hypotension because venodilation reduces preload to a stiff, infarcted RV, dropping cardiac output further.
traps: Pulmonary embolism: also causes RV strain and hypotension, but here the ECG shows inferior ST elevation and troponin rise is from infarction, not strain.
Cardiogenic shock from left ventricular MI: that would show pulmonary edema on exam and chest X-ray, whereas RVMI lungs are clear.
Pericarditis: diffuse ST elevation without reciprocal changes, and hypotension is not a feature unless tamponade develops.
right_ventricular_myocardial_infarction.clue: Jugular venous distention with clear lungs and hypotension after sublingual nitroglycerin.

post_mi_pericarditis_dressler_syndrome.hook: This is an autoimmune-mediated pericardial inflammation triggered by myocardial necrosis—not ongoing ischemia—so the pain arises from fibrinous pericardial friction, not from coronary occlusion.
features: Pleuropericardial chest pain: sharp, positional (worse supine, better leaning forward), and pleuritic (worse with inspiration), due to inflamed pericardial layers rubbing during cardiac and respiratory motion.

Pericardial friction rub: a scratchy, high-frequency sound auscultated best at left lower sternal border with the patient leaning forward—caused by fibrinous exudate coating the visceral and parietal pericardium.

Diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR depression on ECG: concave upward ST elevation in multiple leads (not reciprocal), reflecting diffuse subepicardial inflammation rather than focal transmural ischemia.
traps: Reinfarction: Both cause chest pain and ST elevation, but reinfarction pain is ischemic (pressure-like, not positional) and ST changes are regional with reciprocal depression, not diffuse.
Pulmonary embolism: Pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea overlap, but PE lacks a friction rub, has right heart strain on ECG (S1Q3T3), and D-dimer/CTPA positive.

Acute pericarditis from other causes (viral, uremic): Same mechanism of pericardial inflammation, but Dressler occurs 1–6 weeks post-MI and is immune-mediated, not infectious, so history of recent MI is the key discriminator.
post_mi_pericarditis_dressler_syndrome.clue: Chest pain that is sharp, positional, and pleuritic, with a friction rub on exam, occurring 1–6 weeks after an MI, with diffuse ST elevation and PR depression on ECG.

community_acquired_pneumonia.hook: This is an alveolar filling process where neutrophils and fibrin physically replace air in the distal airspaces, causing the classic consolidation exam and imaging findings.
features: Productive cough with purulent sputum due to neutrophilic exudate filling alveoli and bronchioles.
Bronchial breath sounds and egophony because consolidated lung transmits sound better than air-filled lung.
Lobar opacity on CXR without volume loss, reflecting dense cellular/fibrinous exudate rather than atelectasis.
traps: Pulmonary embolism can cause pleuritic pain and dyspnea but lacks productive cough and consolidation on CXR; the mechanism is vascular occlusion, not alveolar infection.
Lung cancer may cause cough and lobar opacity but is insidious, afebrile, and often shows volume loss or hilar mass due to bronchial obstruction.
community_acquired_pneumonia.clue: Acute onset of fever with a single lobar consolidation on CXR and bronchial breath sounds on exam.

lung_cancer.hook: In lung cancer, the cough is due to an endobronchial mass causing obstruction and post-obstructive pneumonia, not the acute parenchymal infection of CAP.
features: Chronic, non-productive cough that may become productive over weeks to months, often with hemoptysis from tumor erosion into airways.
Constitutional symptoms (weight loss, anorexia, fatigue) from paraneoplastic effects or systemic tumor burden, not acute infection.
Recurrent or non-resolving pneumonia in the same lobe due to persistent bronchial obstruction by the mass.
traps: CAP: acute onset with fever, productive cough, and consolidation on CXR; resolves with antibiotics. Lung cancer has insidious onset, hemoptysis, and failure to clear.
Tuberculosis: chronic cough, hemoptysis, weight loss; but TB has night sweats, apical cavitary lesions, and positive AFB smear/culture.
Bronchiectasis: chronic cough with copious purulent sputum; but has dilated airways on CT and recurrent infections without obstruction.
lung_cancer.clue: Hemoptysis in a smoker with a chronic cough and no fever suggests lung cancer over CAP.

lung_abscess.hook: Lung abscess is a suppurative complication of pneumonia where necrosis creates an air-fluid cavity, not just consolidation.
features: Persistent fever despite antibiotics due to ongoing necrosis and pus accumulation
Foul-smelling sputum from anaerobic metabolism within the abscess cavity
CXR with thick-walled cavity and air-fluid level, not just lobar opacity
traps: Empyema: fluid in pleural space, not lung parenchyma; thoracentesis yields pus but no air-fluid level on CXR
Cavitary lung cancer: irregular, thick walls with nodularity, not acute infection symptoms
lung_abscess.clue: Putrid sputum or failure to defervesce after 72 hours of CAP treatment

bronchitis.hook: Bronchitis is a surface infection of the conducting airways causing cough, but without the alveolar consolidation, systemic toxicity, or focal exam findings that define pneumonia.
features: Cough is typically non-productive or minimally productive with clear/mucoid sputum, not purulent or rusty as in pneumococcal pneumonia.
Fever is low-grade or absent; significant tachypnea, tachycardia, or hypoxemia are absent because gas exchange units are not involved.
Lung exam is clear or shows diffuse wheezes/rhonchi—never localized crackles or bronchial breath sounds as seen with alveolar consolidation.
traps: Acute bronchitis vs. pneumonia: Both cause cough and fever, but bronchitis lacks focal consolidative signs (crackles, egophony, dullness) and CXR shows no infiltrate.
Bronchitis vs. COPD exacerbation: In COPD, the cough is typically chronic with acute worsening, and exam shows hyperinflation and distant breath sounds, not the acute focal findings of pneumonia.
bronchitis.clue: Localized crackles with bronchial breath sounds on exam—these are never present in bronchitis because it spares the alveoli.

pulmonary_embolus.hook: In pulmonary embolus, cough is dry and driven by subpleural ischemia/infarction triggering vagal irritant receptors, not by alveolar consolidation filling with infectious exudate.
features: Pleuritic chest pain with cough but no purulent sputum (unlike CAP's productive cough from neutrophil-laden alveoli)
Dyspnea out of proportion to exam findings (no consolidation crackles or bronchial breath sounds, unlike CAP's lobar physical exam)
Tachycardia and hypoxemia with clear CXR (ventilation-perfusion mismatch from vascular occlusion, not alveolar filling)
traps: Pneumonia: Both cause cough, fever, and pleuritic pain, but PE has no purulent sputum or consolidation on exam/CXR because the pathology is vascular, not alveolar
COPD exacerbation: Both cause dyspnea and hypoxemia, but PE lacks wheezing or prolonged expiration and has sudden pleuritic pain rather than gradual increase in baseline symptoms
Musculoskeletal chest pain: Both can have pleuritic pain, but PE has systemic signs (tachycardia, hypoxemia) from right heart strain and shunt
pulmonary_embolus.clue: Sudden pleuritic chest pain with clear CXR and dyspnea out of proportion to lung exam.

legionella_pneumonia.hook: Legionella is an intracellular pathogen that evades lysosomal fusion, causing a pneumonia with prominent systemic and gastrointestinal features due to cytokine release and direct organ invasion.
features: Cough is often non-productive or minimally productive, unlike the purulent sputum of typical CAP.
High fevers with relative bradycardia (pulse-temperature dissociation) due to bacterial toxin effects on the autonomic nervous system.
Extrapulmonary manifestations like hyponatremia (SIADH from pulmonary inflammation), diarrhea, and confusion from CNS involvement.
traps: It mimics typical CAP (Streptococcus pneumoniae) but lacks purulent sputum and has more GI/neuro symptoms; the mechanism is intracellular vs. extracellular infection.
It can be confused with viral pneumonia (e.g., influenza) but Legionella has a more rapid progression and lobar consolidation on imaging.
Relative bradycardia is often missed; in typical CAP, fever increases heart rate proportionally, but Legionella toxins blunt this response.
legionella_pneumonia.clue: Hyponatremia with diarrhea and confusion in a patient with lobar pneumonia and dry cough.

copd_exacerbation.hook: This is not COPD—COPD exacerbation is a gas-trapping, barrel-chested, prolonged-expiration wheeze, whereas this patient has lobar consolidation, which is a space-occupying, airless, densified lung.
features: Consolidation is a physical replacement of air by pus/fluid in the alveolar space, causing bronchial breath sounds (sound transmits better through solid) and crackles (fluid bubbling).
Fever and pleuritic pain arise from the inflammatory response directly in the lung parenchyma and adjacent pleura, not from airway bronchospasm.
CXR shows lobar opacity with air bronchograms because the alveoli are filled but the larger airways remain patent.
traps: COPD exacerbation: Mechanism is airway inflammation + bronchospasm → trapped air, not alveolar filling. Exam shows wheeze, prolonged expiration, hyperresonance, not consolidation signs.
Lung cancer: Can cause cough and consolidation-like collapse but is usually afebrile, chronic, and lacks acute infectious symptoms. The CXR would show mass effect, not rapid lobar consolidation.
copd_exacerbation.clue: Bronchial breath sounds over the affected area—this is the physical exam hallmark of consolidated lung, not of COPD.

and_bronchiectasis.hook: Bronchiectasis is a structural airway dilation from repeated inflammation, not an acute infection; it causes chronic cough with copious sputum, unlike this acute consolidation with fever and lobar opacity.
features: Chronic daily cough with copious purulent sputum production, not acute-onset
Permanent, irreversible dilation of bronchi due to chronic inflammation and impaired mucociliary clearance
Recurrent infections in the same lung regions, often with clubbing and coarse crackles on exam
traps: Community-acquired pneumonia: acute consolidation from infection, resolves after treatment; bronchiectasis is chronic structural damage that persists between exacerbations
Lung abscess: single cavitary lesion from necrotizing infection, not diffuse bronchial dilation; imaging shows air-fluid level within a cavity
COPD exacerbation: chronic airflow obstruction with acute worsening, but lacks permanent bronchial dilation on HRCT and often has less sputum volume
and_bronchiectasis.clue: A history of recurrent infections in the same lobe with persistent clubbing on exam should raise suspicion for bronchiectasis over acute pneumonia.

pcp_pneumonia_hiv_aids.hook: In PCP, the cough is dry and insidious because the organism fills alveoli with foamy exudate rather than causing the neutrophil-rich consolidation of typical CAP.
features: Dry, non-productive cough (or scant white sputum) due to intra-alveolar foamy exudate without significant neutrophil infiltration
Subacute onset over weeks with progressive dyspnea and exertional hypoxia out of proportion to lung exam (which may be clear or have minimal crackles)
Bilateral diffuse interstitial or ground-glass opacities on CXR (not lobar consolidation) because PCP coats alveolar walls with organisms and exudate
traps: Community-acquired pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae): produces acute productive cough, lobar consolidation on CXR, and neutrophilic infiltrate, whereas PCP is subacute, dry, and interstitial
Pulmonary edema: also causes diffuse bilateral infiltrates and hypoxemia, but PCP has no signs of fluid overload (JVD, S3, peripheral edema) and onset is slower
pcp_pneumonia_hiv_aids.clue: A patient with HIV (or other immunosuppression) presenting with weeks of dry cough and dyspnea, minimal auscultatory findings, and bilateral interstitial infiltrates

tuberculosis.hook: Tuberculosis is a slow-growing, airborne mycobacterial infection that thrives in the oxygen-rich upper lobes, causing a chronic granulomatous inflammation that leads to cavitation—this is not the acute, neutrophil-driven lobar consolidation of CAP.
features: Chronic, insidious cough (weeks to months) with night sweats, weight loss, and hemoptysis, reflecting the slow replication and tissue destruction by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Chest X-ray shows apical or upper lobe infiltrates often with cavitation, as the high oxygen tension in these zones favors mycobacterial growth and granuloma caseation.
Positive acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear and culture from sputum, or a positive interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA), confirming active mycobacterial infection rather than bacterial pneumonia.
traps: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) presents acutely with productive cough, fever, and lobar consolidation on CXR—unlike TB, it is caused by pyogenic bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae that trigger rapid neutrophilic inflammation without granuloma formation or cavitation.

Lung cancer can cause chronic cough, weight loss, and hemoptysis, but its CXR shows a solitary nodule or mass (not apical cavitation) and lacks infectious symptoms like night sweats or fever; biopsy differentiates.
tuberculosis.clue: A chronic cough (>3 weeks) with night sweats and apical cavitation on CXR, especially in an immunocompromised or at-risk patient.

legionella_pneumonia_legionnaires_diseas.hook: Legionella pneumonia is a diagnosis of mechanism: it is a severe, atypical pneumonia caused by inhalation of aerosolized water contaminated with Legionella pneumophila, which infects alveolar macrophages, leading to a robust inflammatory response and multisystem involvement.
features: High fever, often >39°C, with relative bradycardia (pulse-temperature dissociation) due to the organism's toxin interfering with the heart's response to fever.
Dry cough initially, then productive of scanty, non-purulent sputum; prominent gastrointestinal symptoms like diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal pain due to macrophage infection in the gut.
Hyponatremia (low sodium) caused by SIADH from pulmonary inflammation, which is a classic lab clue distinguishing it from typical CAP.
traps: Typical CAP (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae): Both present with cough, fever, and consolidation on CXR, but Legionella has a more systemic presentation (GI symptoms, hyponatremia, relative bradycardia) and lacks purulent sputum and rapid response to beta-lactams.

Influenza pneumonia: Also causes high fever and myalgias, but Legionella has a more gradual onset, prominent GI symptoms, and hyponatremia; influenza often has a rapid onset and is more likely in seasonal outbreaks.
legionella_pneumonia_legionnaires_diseas.clue: A patient with pneumonia who also has diarrhea, confusion, and hyponatremia (Na <130) should immediately trigger consideration of Legionella.

community_acquired_pneumonia.hook: The consolidation on CXR is not just a shadow — it's a physical space filled with neutrophils, fibrin, and edema fluid, replacing air and causing shunt physiology.
features: Productive cough with purulent sputum — neutrophils and bacteria fill alveoli, triggering cough reflex and mucopurulent secretions.
Bronchial breath sounds — consolidated lung transmits sound from large airways directly to the chest wall because airless parenchyma no longer muffles it.
Hypoxemia — alveolar spaces filled with exudate prevent gas exchange, creating right-to-left shunt; supplemental oxygen may not fully correct it.
traps: Lung cancer — mass can also cause consolidation on CXR, but lacks acute fever and purulent sputum; cancer grows slowly, pneumonia evolves over days.
Pulmonary embolism — pleuritic pain and dyspnea mimic pneumonia, but PE has no productive cough or lobar consolidation; instead, it shows wedge-shaped infarct on CXR later.
Bronchiectasis — chronic cough with purulent sputum, but crackles are coarse and persistent, not focal; CXR shows tram-track lines, not acute lobar consolidation.
community_acquired_pneumonia.clue: Lobar consolidation on CXR with acute fever and productive cough — the alveolar space is filled, not just inflamed.

lung_cancer.hook: Airspace filling by neutrophils and proteinaceous exudate—not by malignant cells—drives this acute lobar consolidation with fever and purulent sputum.
features: Acute onset of productive cough, fever, and dyspnea reflects rapid neutrophil recruitment into alveoli, a hallmark of bacterial pneumonia.
Bronchial breath sounds and crackles over the affected lobe arise from consolidated lung transmitting sound more efficiently, contrasting with the typically absent or dulled sounds of a mass.

Lobar consolidation on CXR is a silhouette sign of airspace opacification, which in pneumonia is homogeneous and lobar, while lung cancer often presents as a irregular, spiculated nodule or mass with post-obstructive changes.
traps: Lung cancer: presents insidiously with chronic cough, weight loss, hemoptysis; consolidation is rare unless post-obstructive pneumonia develops, and fever is less prominent without infection.
Lung abscess: features cavitation with air-fluid level on CXR and foul sputum, driven by anaerobic infection and necrosis, not acute consolidation.
Bronchiectasis: chronic cough with copious purulent sputum and recurrent infections, but CXR shows tram-track opacities and dilated airways, not acute lobar consolidation.
lung_cancer.clue: Acute fever and pleuritic chest pain with a single lobar consolidation on CXR in an elderly patient with hypoxia and hyponatremia point to severe CAP, not lung cancer.

lung_abscess.hook: A lung abscess is a cavity of necrotic lung tissue from aspiration or severe infection, not just consolidation like in CAP.
features: Putrid sputum from anaerobic bacteria (e.g., Bacteroides) digesting tissue, a hallmark not seen in typical CAP.
Chest X-ray or CT shows a thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level, distinct from the homogeneous lobar consolidation of CAP.
Prolonged, indolent course with weight loss and night sweats, unlike the acute onset of CAP.
traps: CAP can cavitate (e.g., Klebsiella, Staph aureus) but lacks putrid sputum and thick-walled cavity.
Lung cancer can cavitate but has irregular walls, no air-fluid level, and no fever or putrid sputum.
Empyema has air-fluid level but is pleural, not parenchymal, and lacks putrid sputum.
lung_abscess.clue: A history of aspiration or poor dentition with foul-smelling sputum on exam.

bronchitis.hook: Bronchitis causes inflammation of the large airways without alveolar involvement, producing a dry or minimally productive cough without the consolidation findings seen in pneumonia.
features: Cough is typically non-productive or with scant clear sputum, reflecting airway irritation without alveolar exudate.
Absence of crackles, bronchial breath sounds, or dullness on exam, as the lung parenchyma is spared.
No fever or only low-grade fever, since systemic response is limited to airway inflammation without parenchymal infection.
traps: Pneumonia: Both can cause cough and fever, but pneumonia shows focal crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and consolidative opacity on CXR due to alveolar filling with pus/fluid.
COPD exacerbation: Presents with increased dyspnea, wheezing, and history of smoking, but lacks focal consolidation; mechanism is bronchospasm and mucus hypersecretion, not parenchymal infection.
Bronchiectasis: Chronic cough with copious purulent sputum and clubbing, due to permanent airway dilation and impaired clearance, not acute lobar consolidation.
bronchitis.clue: On exam, listen for bronchial breath sounds and crackles over a specific lobe — these indicate consolidation (pneumonia), not bronchitis.

pulmonary_embolus.hook: In pulmonary embolus, cough and pleuritic pain arise from subpleural infarction or ischemia, not from alveolar consolidation like in pneumonia.
features: Sudden-onset dyspnea and pleuritic pain without purulent sputum or high fever
Exam may show tachypnea, tachycardia, and occasionally a pleural rub, but not consolidation findings like bronchial breath sounds
CXR is often normal or shows atelectasis, effusion, or wedge-shaped opacity—never lobar consolidation
traps: Pneumonia: Both cause cough, fever, and pleuritic pain, but pneumonia produces purulent sputum and consolidation on exam/CXR; PE does not
Musculoskeletal chest pain: Can mimic pleuritic pain but lacks tachypnea, hypoxia, or any cough/fever response
pulmonary_embolus.clue: Acute dyspnea with pleuritic chest pain and a normal CXR or one showing only atelectasis/effusion, especially with risk factors like recent surgery or immobility

legionella_pneumonia.hook: Legionella pneumonia is a 'systemic intracellular infection' that invades alveolar macrophages, causing a severe pneumonia with prominent extrapulmonary features—unlike typical Streptococcus pneumoniae which is a 'surface extracellular pathogen' triggering a brisk neutrophilic response confined to the airway.
features: High fever, relative bradycardia, and dry cough (initially) due to intracellular replication within macrophages, which blunts the typical purulent sputum production seen with extracellular bacteria like Strep pneumoniae.

Prominent gastrointestinal symptoms (diarrhea, abdominal pain) and neurologic changes (confusion, headache) because Legionella disseminates hematogenously, affecting multiple organ systems—unlike pneumococcus which stays largely in the lung.

Hyponatremia (SIADH-like) and elevated liver enzymes, reflecting the systemic inflammatory response and direct organ invasion by the intracellular pathogen, not seen with typical lobar consolidation from Strep pneumoniae.
traps: It mimics severe Strep pneumoniae pneumonia on CXR (lobar consolidation), but Legionella's dry cough, GI symptoms, and hyponatremia are key differentiators—pneumococcus produces copious purulent sputum and no SIADH.

It can look like influenza with high fever and myalgias, but influenza is seasonal, has abrupt onset of sore throat and nasal congestion, and lacks the GI/neurologic findings and hyponatremia of Legionella.

It may be confused with Mycoplasma pneumonia (atypical presentation), but Mycoplasma typically has a gradual onset, prominent headache, and cold agglutinins, whereas Legionella is more acute, severe, and associated with water aerosol exposure.
legionella_pneumonia.clue: Ask about recent exposure to hot tubs, air conditioning cooling towers, or hotel showers—if positive, Legionella is the likely cause of this 'atypical' pneumonia with systemic features.

copd_exacerbation.hook: In COPD exacerbation, the core mechanism is dynamic airway collapse and mucus hypersecretion causing ventilation-perfusion mismatch, not parenchymal consolidation from infection.
features: Wheezing and prolonged expiration due to bronchospasm and loss of elastic recoil
Purulent sputum and increased dyspnea from neutrophilic inflammation and mucus plugging
Hyperinflation on CXR (flattened diaphragms, increased AP diameter) without focal consolidation
traps: Community acquired pneumonia: consolidation from alveolar infection causes crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and lobar opacity on CXR, whereas COPD exacerbation shows diffuse wheezes and hyperinflation
copd_exacerbation.clue: In COPD exacerbation, the cough is typically chronic with acute worsening, and exam reveals diffuse wheezes rather than focal crackles or bronchial breath sounds.

and_bronchiectasis.hook: In CAP, alveolar airspace is replaced by exudates causing consolidation; in bronchiectasis, permanent bronchial dilation from chronic inflammation leads to impaired mucociliary clearance and recurrent infections.
features: Persistent, copious purulent sputum production due to dilated airways with impaired clearance
Recurrent exacerbations from bacterial colonization (e.g., Pseudomonas) and impaired mucociliary function
Coarse crackles and wheezes on exam from airway secretions, not alveolar consolidation
traps: Chronic bronchitis (COPD): also has chronic cough and sputum but lacks permanent structural dilation—bronchiectasis shows bronchial dilation on HRCT and more severe recurrent infections
and_bronchiectasis.clue: Acute onset with lobar consolidation on CXR and bronchial breath points to infectious consolidation (CAP), not chronic structural dilation.

pcp_pneumonia_hiv_aids.hook: Unlike typical lobar consolidation from Streptococcus pneumoniae, PCP pneumonia in HIV/AIDS causes a diffuse interstitial process because the organism directly injures the alveolar-capillary membrane, leading to impaired gas exchange without focal consolidation.
features: Subacute onset of dry cough, fever, and progressive dyspnea over weeks, reflecting gradual alveolar filling with foamy exudate rather than sudden bacterial invasion.
CXR shows bilateral interstitial or ground-glass opacities, not lobar consolidation—because PCP triggers a diffuse inflammatory response along alveolar septa.
Severe hypoxemia out of proportion to exam findings due to thickened alveolar-capillary barrier causing V/Q mismatch and diffusion block.
traps: Community-acquired pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae) presents with acute onset, productive cough, and lobar consolidation on CXR because bacteria cause rapid neutrophil recruitment and intra-alveolar exudate.
Pulmonary edema shows similar diffuse interstitial pattern but lacks fever and has frothy sputum; mechanism is hydrostatic or permeability-driven, not infectious.
Miliary TB can produce diffuse nodules but is usually more chronic with night sweats and weight loss; granulomas are nodular, not ground-glass.
pcp_pneumonia_hiv_aids.clue: A non-productive cough with profound hypoxemia and bilateral interstitial infiltrates in an immunocompromised patient—especially if CD4 <200—should trigger immediate consideration of PCP.

legionella_pneumonia_legionnaires_diseas.hook: Legionella is an intracellular pathogen that hijacks alveolar macrophages, causing a severe pneumonia with prominent systemic and extrapulmonary features due to its toxin and inflammatory cascade.
features: High fever (>39°C) with relative bradycardia — the systemic inflammatory response is intense but the heart rate fails to proportionally increase due to bacterial toxins or cytokine effects.
Multilobar or patchy infiltrates on CXR that may worsen despite antibiotics, reflecting ongoing macrophage infection and necrosis rather than simple airspace filling.
